Changelog

Recent roam-code releases — see who builds it or jump to the v13 narrative in the README. Full history at CHANGELOG.md on GitHub.

All notable changes to roam-code will be documented in this file.

The format is based on Keep a Changelog, and this project adheres to Semantic Versioning.

[Unreleased]

Fixed

  • side-effects certified a symbol pure at confidence HIGH from a file it never opened, and said partial_success: false beside it. Measured on a two-symbol scratch repo (wipe_workspace calling os.system, plus add): readable, the command reports 1 none, 1 process; deny read on the one file with icacls /deny -- which changes neither mtime nor size, so no reindex is triggered -- and the same command reports Classified 2 symbols: 2 none, both at confidence: high, each carrying the evidence string "no outgoing calls, no patterns, no risky imports", with state: ok, partial_success: false, and the agent fact "side-effects scan confirmed 2 symbols are pure (no detected side effects)". That is an affirmative denial of evidence nobody looked for. classify_side_effects read each file once and, on a missing path or an OSError, set the body to "" and discarded the outcome; Layers 2 and 3 then observed nothing and the classifier fell to its "confident this is pure" branch. Layer 1 cannot compensate: measured on roam-code's own 18k-symbol DB, zero os. and zero subprocess. symbols are indexed, and the callee join is an inner join on symbols, so the file read is the ONLY detector for stdlib sinks -- losing it loses 100% of that signal while RAISING confidence. The per-file read outcome is now retained as read / missing / unreadable and threaded into the classifier: a symbol whose source was never read and whose call edges proved nothing is kinds: ["unknown"], confidence: "low" with the reason naming the read failure and the path. Layer 1 still runs and still returns process at high confidence from a resolved edge with no body at all -- gating the whole classifier on the read would have deleted the one detector that does not need it. The switch is deliberately the read OUTCOME and not body == "": a stale index whose line_start points past EOF yields an empty slice from a perfectly readable file, which is a staleness problem with its own disclosure, and a test pins that such a file still classifies none. A new classify_side_effects_status returns (classifications, coverage) carrying files_discovered / files_read / files_unreadable / files_missing / symbols_source_unavailable -- the load_tenant_guard_signals_status split already in this repo -- and classify_side_effects stays the thin list-returning wrapper, so all twelve world-model consumers are untouched. roam side-effects publishes those counts plus scan_incomplete, sets partial_success and state from the same boolean the text channel reads, names the denominator in the verdict, and stops emitting "confirmed N symbols are pure" whenever the scan was incomplete. Every consumer emits strictly fewer findings after this, so no honest roam verify run newly fails. What this does not close: the pattern catalogue anchors only Python and JS/TS while roam indexes 20+ languages, so a Go, Rust, Java, Ruby or C# body is read successfully, matches nothing, and is STILL published as none at high confidence -- measured on a Go+Ruby scratch repo where exec.Command("rm","-rf"), os.Create and a backtick rm -rf all report 7 none, high. That is the same defect with a different cause and a contract-level fix (it inverts the headline for ~18 of the indexed languages and turns roam idempotency from idempotent to unknown on all of them), so it is deliberately left open rather than folded in here. Nothing yet disclosed the language coverage of the catalogue either.
  • The quality gate published true — and the PR comment read "Quality Gate: PASSED" — for a gate where zero expressions could be evaluated. evaluate_gate computed passed from the failure list alone and never consulted checked_expressions, which the same dict already carried. Measured: a results directory holding a health envelope with no health_score, gated on health_score>=70, warns twice and prints true, exit 0. The composite action captures that stdout, writes gate-passed=true, and pr-comment.js mapped anything that was not the literal string false to PASSED — including the empty string a skipped or crashed gate step leaves behind. The partial case is worse than the total one, because a real number is published beside the expressions nobody checked: on a repository's first CI run, with a one-element trend history, direction(health_score)!=worsening,delta(health_score)>=-5,latest(health_score)>=70 evaluates exactly one of three and still publishes true as the verdict for all three. The evaluator now reports a third state. passed keeps its historical "no expression FAILED" meaning so the failure axis stays byte-compatible, and a new state field is failed / unevaluated / passed, with unchecked_expressions naming how many expressions found no payload; main() prints true / false / unknown, and an expression that matched no payload is now an ::error:: rather than a ::warning:: — the user asked for that gate and did not get it. The action validates the widened but still closed token set, publishes a paired gate-state output, and the PR comment renders NOT EVALUATED for both unknown and the empty string. unknown does not fail the job by default, and that default is the measured part: _compute_slope and _metric_delta both need two snapshots, so every adopter's first trend-gated run would go red on a run where nothing is wrong and nothing they can do fixes it except wait — teams that want it to block set the new gate-strict: true, which is routed through the same validate-inputs boundary as every other flag rather than interpolated raw. The behaviour that shipped was enshrined by a test asserting passed is True with checked_expressions == 0; that test is now the one that names the defect. What this does not close: gate-passed remains a boolean and an existing consumer reading only that output still cannot see the third state, so gate-state has to be adopted deliberately; and expressions are still matched against payloads by trial, so a metric misspelled in the gate is indistinguishable from a metric the run legitimately did not produce.
  • roam --sarif health shipped 50 of 60 god components to Code Scanning without saying it had capped the list, while the JSON and text channels both said so. Measured on a generated repo of 60 modules, each a hub calling 25 leaves, so 60 symbols exceed the god-component degree threshold against a list cap of 50: roam health prints "top 50 of 60 god components", roam --json health publishes warnings_out: ['health_god_components_list_capped:showing_top_50_of_60'] with partial_success: true, and roam --sarif health emits 50 results, exits 0, writes nothing to stderr, and produces a document with no invocations, no toolExecutionNotifications and no properties. A Code Scanning consumer saw a complete-looking census that was missing ten findings. The cap is computed in the shared prologue that all three channels run, and is merged into the JSON and text outputs; the SARIF tail simply was not wired to it. It now projects the same bucket through roam.output.sarif.with_sarif_disclosures -- the canonical W1331 adapter that eleven other commands already use -- and writes the marker to stderr as well, matching the text channel without touching stdout. That adapter returns the document untouched on an empty bucket, so every uncapped repository's SARIF is byte-identical to before, and a negative control asserts it carries no invocations key at all. The cap itself is unchanged and the run still exits 0: uncapping would change the reported issue count on every repo at once and make every stored baseline snapshot read as a phantom regression, and a non-zero exit would break the SARIF upload in all five bundled CI templates plus the composite action, on every repository with more than 50 god components. This mattered because six existing tests all reached health through --json, so no test had ever looked at the SARIF channel. What this does not close: the sibling bottleneck cap shares the same marker family and the same fix, but no shipped template redirects a saturated bottleneck list, so it is covered only by the parity test here; and nothing structurally prevents the next command that gains a truncation site from disclosing it on two channels out of three.
  • The fitness rules roam init wrote into every new repository were addressed to a vocabulary no checker reads: one was inert, the other fired on everything. The template wrote threshold: 30 on the complexity rule, but _check_cognitive_complexity_metric reads max and defaults it to 999 -- measured on a fifteen-line file, a function at cognitive complexity 377 PASSED a rule whose own reason string says "Functions above 30 cognitive complexity need refactoring". The same template wrote source: / forbidden_target: on the dependency rule, but _check_dependency_rule reads from / to, both defaulting to **, so the rule forbade every edge in the repository: on a two-function, zero-defect repo that roam init had just created, roam preflight named that rule the risk driver, and roam --json fitness published it as a HIGH-confidence violation beside config_state: "ok" and partial_success: false. Neither spelling belongs to any roam schema -- .roam-rules.yml, read by pr-analyze, uses source_glob / forbidden_target_glob -- so the template was a mangled half-copy of a sibling vocabulary, and the first rule was named for a check a dependency rule cannot perform at all (circular imports are metric: cycles). Both starter templates (roam init and roam fitness --init) now use the keys the dispatched checker actually reads, and the loader names every key nothing reads, plus the dependency rule that constrains neither end of the edge. That disclosure is a WARNING, deliberately: roam init writes the file only when absent, so every repo that has ever run it still carries threshold: 30 on disk, and teaching the checker to read threshold would switch a dormant complexity gate ON across the whole estate at upgrade time with no user action -- a test now asserts that alias is still absent. Warnings flip summary.partial_success and cannot change an exit code, which is computed from failed/errored alone, so no honest run newly fails. Also fixed: six rule["name"] bare subscripts that raised KeyError on a rule with no name, where every sibling used rule.get("name", "unnamed"). What this does not close: an existing .roam/fitness.yaml is never rewritten, so those users get a warning and must edit the file themselves; a dependency rule with neither from nor to still runs (and still forbids every edge) rather than being refused as an ERROR row, because refusing it would flip a currently-passing run red for anyone whose graph happens to have no matching edges -- that escalation is a deliberate open decision; and a rule-level severity: field is documented in this file's own header but is read by nothing, since no checker copies it onto the violations _fitness_classify inspects.
  • The drop-in agent-review workflow roam ships to other people rejected every verdict roam can produce. The Run pr-analyze step in src/roam/templates/ci/agent-review.yml validated summary.verdict by exact set-membership against {INTENTIONAL, SAFE, REVIEW, BLOCK, NOCHANGES}, but pr-analyze has never written a bare token there: it composes the canonical standalone-parse sentence SAFE (risk_level low). Measured on a two-commit scratch repo with a twelve-line diff, running the template's own commands verbatim: pr-analyze exits 0 and writes SAFE (risk_level low), and the validator heredoc then exits 1 with invalid or missing pr-analyze verdict, publishing nothing to $GITHUB_OUTPUT. Every adopter's workflow was red on a clean, SAFE pull request. The validator now parses the canonical sentence with an anchored fullmatch over both closed vocabularies -- the verdict set plus NOCHANGES, and the four canonical risk levels -- and publishes the bare token so the downstream Gate merge on BLOCK case statement works unchanged. The anchoring is the point: the degraded floor sentence pr-analyze completed (risk_level low), which pr-analyze emits when the verdict could not be composed at all, still fails the step, as do UNSAFE (risk_level low), a bare SAFE, an unknown risk tier and a truncated envelope. pr-analyze additionally publishes summary.verdict_code, the machine-readable mirror of the token, derived through that same expression so it is absent exactly when the sentence degraded -- a consumer reading the mirror inherits the same refusal rather than a stale SAFE. The reason this shipped is the shape being corrected: the guard asserted the refusal string was PRESENT in the template and never once ran it. The replacement extracts the heredoc from the shipped YAML and executes it, against synthetic envelopes and against an envelope a real pr-analyze run produced; on the pre-fix template 27 of those assertions fail. What this does not close: the workflow still installs a pinned published roam, so verdict_code only reaches adopters at the next release and the regex remains the load-bearing parse; the other four shipped CI templates were not audited for the same claim-versus-emitter drift; and nothing yet checks that a template's pinned roam version can actually produce the outputs the template consumes.
  • The command whose entire job is reporting syntax was harsher than the one that reports it incidentally. roam verify learned not to call a type-position import('...') with a postfix a syntax error -- the bundled tree-sitter grammar cannot parse that construct, which is a limitation of this build and not a defect in the user's file. roam syntax-check never received the same accommodation, so on the identical source the dedicated tool reported an error and the incidental one did not. A user who ran the specific command to check syntax got the wrong answer, and a user who ran the general one got the right one. The accommodation now lives in parser_pack, beside the parser whose gap it describes, rather than inside either command -- it is a property of the grammar, not of a caller, and keeping one implementation is why the next consumer cannot inherit the old behaviour by omission. Both callers share it; verify's helper is now a thin wrapper. Measured on the same file: syntax-check exits 0 with 0 errors where it previously reported one, verify still scores syntax 100, and a genuine unclosed bracket in the same shape still exits 5 and still names line 2 -- the mask substitutes an identifier of identical byte length precisely so a real error keeps its true coordinates. Fail-before demonstrated by disabling the retry and watching valid TypeScript exit 5 again. What this does not close: it remains an accommodation for ONE measured construct, so the next thing the grammar cannot parse is still reported as broken code by both commands; and Apex is still parsed with the Java grammar, which reports every idiomatic Apex class as containing syntax errors -- roam's own extractor documents that gap and then blames it on the user.
  • roam ai-ratio published "92 files with anomalous comment density" from a 200-row sample of a 4,966-file corpus, with no denominator and no cap disclosure. _comment_density_rows selects every file with line_count > 0; _sample_comment_densities then slices [:200] by rowid and drops any file that raises OSError/UnicodeDecodeError or has fewer than 5 lines. The resulting count sat in signals beside four genuinely whole-corpus signals with nothing naming its population, while --help calls the command "codebase-wide". Measured on roam-code's own index: 4,966 eligible rows, 198 densities actually measured, 92 anomalous -- a 46% in-sample ratio that saturates the score at 1.0, against the 1.9% a reader computes from 92/4,966. The envelope now carries anomalous_files_in_sample, files_measured, files_eligible, sample_cap, sample_capped and sample_ordering, and the text line reads "92 of 198 sampled files anomalous (200-file cap by rowid; 4966 eligible)". The ordering is NAMED rather than randomised on purpose: randomising would move the published number on every run over an unchanged tree, and a disclosed non-representative slice beats a silent one. Separately, fewer than 5 readable densities used to return 0.0 and still carry its full 0.15 weight into the headline ratio -- an absent measurement pushing the estimate DOWN as if it were evidence of human authorship. That case is now marked computable: false, excluded from the weighted average with the remaining weights renormalised, and named in both channels; its published weight becomes 0 while nominal_weight keeps the constant. anomalous_files is retained as an alias so a consumer does not break on the same release that tells it the number meant something narrower. Measured after the change: the ratio on roam-code is unmoved at 0.70, because with all five signals computable the weights already sum to 1.0. What this does not close: confidence is still derived from commit count alone and is not degraded by low file coverage -- a saturated score from a 4% slice still carries HIGH. Changing what that published label MEANS is a semantic change for every user and is left as an owner decision; the coverage numbers it would need are now in the envelope. The 200-file cap itself is unchanged.
  • roam diagnose stamped partial_success: false on an envelope whose own warnings_out named a sqlite OperationalError, and the text channel never mentioned it at all. _iso_summary set partial_success: True and then merged **resolution_block on the next lines; for an exact match resolution_disclosure("symbol") returns partial_success = ("symbol" != "symbol") = False, so the last key won and the True was overwritten -- on both the summary and the top-level mirror. The comment three lines above asserted "partial_success is already True here", and formatter.py's own docstring listed cmd_diagnose (W1244) as "no pre-existing flag -> direct merge"; both were false for this branch, which is exactly how a stale reference entry launders a defect. Measured on a normal indexed repo whose index.db then had ALTER TABLE edges RENAME TO edges_gone applied: roam --json diagnose beta returned partial_success: false alongside warnings_out: ["diagnose_build_graph_failed:OperationalError:no such table: edges"] and target_metrics.out_degree: 1 -- a symbol reported as "not connected in the dependency graph" in the same envelope that gives it a callee -- while the text channel printed only that verdict plus a tip to run roam index, a statement about the USER'S CODE for a failure in roam's own store. The branch now OR-combines instead of direct-merging, exactly as cmd_impact (W1242) and cmd_trace (W1248) already do, and the text branch echoes the same warnings bucket the JSON branch publishes. The reference-adopter line in formatter.py is corrected rather than left to certify the old shape. Controls pin that a healthy run and a genuinely-isolated symbol on a healthy graph are NOT marked partial. What this does not close: the text/JSON exit-code divergence on this path (text 1, json 0) is pinned as deliberate in tests/data/disclosure_asymmetry_baseline.json and is untouched; and the verdict string still says "not connected in the dependency graph" when the real cause is that there is no graph -- the disclosure now travels beside it rather than replacing it.
  • roam pr-analyze --gate published state no_changes for a diff it could not read, which refuted the written justification for its own exemption. cmd_diff consumed the bare get_changed_files, so a failed git diff produced the same empty list as a clean tree and the same state: "no_changes" envelope; pr-analyze reads that state to decide whether a PR is empty, so a substrate failure arrived at the gate as the affirmative fact that there is nothing to review. Measured in a repo with a modified tracked file and a corrupt GIT_INDEX_FILE: roam --json pr-analyze --gate returned {"state": "no_changes", "reasons": ["no changes to analyze"], "rule_violations": 0, "high_severity_critique": 0, "blast_radius": 0, "verdict": "NOCHANGES (risk_level low)"} at exit 0, and the text channel was identical. cmd_diff now emits state: "diff_unavailable" with summary.git_error and partial_success: true when git could not answer, which routes pr-analyze through its existing diff_failed path, and --gate refuses on that state as well as on BLOCK -- on the cached-replay path too, so a replay cannot turn a refusal back into an authorization. A genuinely empty PR still reports NOCHANGES and still exits 0, pinned as a control. This also corrects a paragraph in tests/test_gate_channel_exit_parity.py that exempted pr-analyze on the grounds that its no_changes was "a real answer rather than an absent measurement": the state did not distinguish the two, so the exemption rested on a property the command did not have. Four strict-xfail pins the repo had already written against cmd_diff's half of this defect graduate on their own stated exit conditions. What this does not close: roam diff itself is report-only and still exits 0 on the degraded path -- only its STATE changed, and giving it a gate flag is a separate decision; and cmd_attest, cmd_test_gaps, cmd_affected_tests and cmd_affected still call the bare helper and keep their pins.
  • roam attest capped fitness violations at 50 and then reported the capped number as the violation count in the signed attestation. _collect_fitness_evidence slices violations[:50], and _compute_verdict derived the reported number with len(fitness_data["violations"]) -- over the TRUNCATED list. The evidence block carried only {rules, violations}: no total, no truncated flag, no cap disclosure anywhere in the envelope, and with --sign that number is content-hashed into a tamper-evident artifact. Measured on roam-code's own index with every indexed file in scope and the repo's own .roam/fitness.yaml: the checker returned 909 violations, the attestation carried 50, the verdict warning read "50 fitness violations in changed files" and the text section header read "FITNESS VIOLATIONS (50):". _collect_test_evidence in the SAME module already gets this right -- it caps tests[:50] and publishes selected: len(test_results) -- so the correct shape was one function away. The evidence now carries violations_total and violations_truncated; the verdict and the rendered header count the measurement, and the section adds "(evidence carries the first 50 of 909)" so a reader cannot mistake the list for the total. The cap itself is kept: an attestation that grows without bound is its own problem, and the defect was that the cap was UNDISCLOSED. Older payloads without the field still compute, pinned by a test, because the attestation format is consumed by other tools and a KeyError would turn a disclosure fix into an outage. What this does not close: the same 50-item cap applies to the JSON evidence list, so a consumer wanting every violation still has to run roam fitness itself; and this is a warning, not a gate -- attest does not fail on fitness violations at any count, which is a separate decision.
  • roam verify --report returned PASS 100 with verification_complete: true over a tracked file that does not parse, because its coverage repair also honours the 1 MB discovery cap. Commit b4dcf835 closed the case where report mode scored a whole-repo verdict over a partial index; that repair enumerates candidates with discover_files, which applies the indexer's size cap, so an OVERSIZED tracked source file is never counted as missing, never triggers the light reindex, and never reaches a check. Measured on a repo of ok.py plus a 1.4 MB broken_big.py with a genuine syntax error at line 200001, both git add-ed: roam verify --report returned verdict PASS, score 100, files_checked 1, verification_complete true, partial_success false, violation_count 0, exit 0, while ast.parse on that file raises and SELECT path FROM files returns only ok.py. Report mode now treats a size-skipped tracked CODE file as an unverified file: it is named in a hard-blocking verification gap, verification_complete drops to false, state becomes verification_incomplete, and incomplete_reasons carries oversized_target_unverified. This REFUSES where the sibling secrets fix RECOVERS, and the asymmetry is the point: a regex sweep does not need the index, so secrets can simply read the file, whereas verify's checks run over symbol rows, graph edges and metrics -- there is nothing to recover while the file exceeds the indexer's bound, so the honest answer is to say so. The gap is scoped to code surfaces; a 2 MB CHANGELOG or JSON fixture is not a verification gap, and measured on roam-code itself all three of its oversized tracked files are non-code, so this repo's own report verdict is unchanged -- pinned by a control. What this does not close: the file still cannot be verified. Raising or removing the indexer cap is a separate decision with a real cost, and verify <path> on an oversized file remains as blind as it was -- only the whole-repo claim of coverage is corrected.
  • The 1 MB discovery cap made roam secrets --fail-on-found exit 0 over a tracked file holding a live-shaped AWS key. _filter_files dropped any path over MAX_FILE_SIZE with a bare continue, so the file was in NEITHER the discovered set nor the indexed set and _count_unindexed -- which computes discovered - indexed -- subtracted it to zero. Measured on two tracked files, small.py (39 B, no credential) and big.py (1.4 MB, AKIA... on its last line): roam index && roam secrets --fail-on-found printed "VERDICT: No secrets found (1 files scanned)" at exit 0, with files_filtered 0, files_undiscoverable 0, files_unindexed 0, files_unreadable 0, scan_incomplete false, partial_success false. Positive control: the identical key in the 39-byte file IS reported, so the pattern fires -- only the oversized file was invisible. Commit 93f9655e chose discover_files as the yardstick on the premise that "files discovery deliberately excludes are not blind spots", which is true of generated artefacts (a scope decision) and false of a resource cap (roam declining to look). Discovery now returns its size skips through discover_files_with_skips, and secrets RECOVERS them: the 1 MB bound is an INDEXER bound -- building a symbol graph over a multi-megabyte file is expensive, a line-oriented regex sweep is not -- so the honest fix is to measure what the verdict claims rather than refuse to answer. The key in the 1.4 MB file is now reported at its correct line. A second, much larger scanner bound still applies and, unlike the first, is LOUD: a file past it is named, counted in files_oversized_unscanned, published in oversized_unscanned_paths, and makes --fail-on-found refuse. Neither cap was raised. Measured on roam-code itself: 3 tracked files exceed 1 MB (CHANGELOG.md, the generated changelog.html, one JSON fixture), all three are now read, and the scan still finds nothing -- so the repo's own CI gate is unchanged; a control pins that a repo with no oversized files stays partial_success: false. What this does not close: only secrets recovers the skipped files. Every other consumer of discover_files still silently inherits the cap, and the skips are computed per call rather than recorded by the indexer, so a command wanting the same coverage pays for a second discovery walk.
  • roam calc-inventory --fail-on-divergence exited 0 with "no calculations found" over a corpus where every file failed to open. files_scanned was len(_discover_files(root)) -- the paths rglob yielded -- while the actual read happens inside extract_calcs_from_file, whose docstring says "[] on any I/O or grammar miss". The caller could not tell an empty result from an unopened file, so the opt-in CI gate computed its PASS over the empty set of files it decoded while publishing the count of files it merely listed. Measured on two Python files each holding a rounded money formula, with read access denied on both: --json returned calculations: 0, files_scanned: 2, gate_failed: false, partial_success: false, verdict: "no calculations found" at exit 0, and the text channel agreed. Baseline with both readable: 2 calculations across 2 files. The extractor now returns (calcs, status) with read / unreadable / no_language; the command counts files_read apart from files_discovered, publishes both plus files_unreadable, files_unknown_language, scan_incomplete, partial_success and the skipped paths, and reports cannot certify — 0 of 2 files read (2 unreadable). --fail-on-divergence exits 5 on an incomplete read in BOTH channels. This gate fails closed where the sibling magic-numbers fix only discloses, and the asymmetry is deliberate: a magic-number finding is a property of one file, so an unread file can only ADD occurrences, whereas a divergence is a property of the RELATION between two formulas sharing a field name -- the undecoded file may hold the second formula that makes the first divergent, so an unread file can RETRACT this command's answer. The divergence rule itself was not weakened. Fixing this exposed a second defect in the same command: the text channel's gate exit sat BELOW an if not calcs: return, so a zero-calculation refusal would have exited 0 in text while --json exited 5 -- the channel split this repo has now corrected three times. Controls pin that a fully-read corpus still passes in both channels, and that without --fail-on-divergence an incomplete read is disclosed rather than refused.
  • roam magic-numbers said "0 magic numbers across N files scanned" when N files were discovered and zero were parsed. files_scanned was len(_discover_files(root)) -- the count of paths rglob YIELDED -- and was never decremented by a file the scanner could not open or could not parse. _scan_python_file returned [] on OSError and [] on SyntaxError, and the tree-sitter scanner did the same, so "unreadable", "unparseable" and "genuinely clean" arrived at the aggregator as the identical empty list. The denominator admitted the files the numerator could never see. Measured on two syntactically broken Python files each holding a repeated numeric literal: roam magic-numbers <dir> --threshold 1 printed "VERDICT: 0 magic numbers across 2 files scanned" and exited 0, with summary.partial_success: false. The control -- the same literals with valid syntax -- reported 2 magic numbers, so the corpus was not devoid of them. --help disclosed nothing about skipped, unreadable or unparseable inputs. Both scanners now return the occurrence list plus a status, the command counts files_read separately from files_discovered, and the empty verdict names its own denominator: "0 magic numbers across 0 of 2 files read (2 unparseable)". The envelope carries files_discovered, files_read, files_unreadable, files_unparseable, scan_incomplete and partial_success, plus the skipped paths themselves, and the text channel lists them. The shape is the one this repo already ships in cmd_article_12_check. No threshold was lowered and the SyntaxError guard is still there -- an unread file can only ADD occurrences, never retract one, so the fix is to say what was read. A fully-read corpus with no findings still reports "0 magic numbers across 2 files scanned" with partial_success: false, pinned as a control. What this does not close: magic-numbers has no gate flag, so there is no exit code to change and none is invented -- if a gate is ever added it must consult scan_incomplete. And the tree-sitter path has no unparseable state: when the grammar is missing the regex sweep still READS the file, so a grammar-shaped blind spot there is a precision question rather than a coverage one, and is untouched.
  • roam docs-coverage --threshold reported 100.0% and passed its gate having measured zero symbols. _compute_coverage hard-coded if total <= 0: return 0, 0, 100.0 -- an empty denominator became the exact value that means perfect, and the gate then compared 100.0 against the caller's bar and passed. Coverage over an empty set is UNKNOWN, not 100%. Measured in a repository of real, indexed Python source in which every symbol is underscore-prefixed, so the export-marker criterion selects none of them: roam docs-coverage --threshold 95 printed "Coverage: 100.0%" and exited 0, and --json asserted coverage_pct: 100.0, gate_passed: true, partial_success: false, public_symbols: 0. --help promises exit 5 below the threshold. The sibling gate in the same directory on the same index already refuses -- roam py-types --ci --min-coverage 95 prints "GATE FAILED: type coverage not computable (no_public_python_functions)" and exits 5 -- so this is that decision one command over. _compute_coverage now returns None for the percentage when there is no denominator, --threshold refuses with GATE FAILED: doc coverage not computable (no_public_symbols) and exit 5 in BOTH channels, and the envelope carries coverage_pct: null, coverage_pct_computable: false, state: no_public_symbols and partial_success: true so a consumer can tell "I measured 50% and your bar is 99" from "I could not measure anything". No threshold moved. Reporting mode without --threshold still exits 0 -- nobody asked that run to certify anything -- and a repo with real public symbols still gates on its real number. What this does not close: both channels agreed on the wrong answer, so the differential sweep's exit-code-parity law could not have seen this, and the pair was never probed at all because tests/test_gate_channel_exit_parity.py enumerates BOOLEAN flags only, as its own docstring says. Extending that harness to value-bearing thresholds (--threshold, --fail-under, --min-coverage) is NOT done here: it needs a per-option decision about which value is maximally demanding -- 100 for a coverage floor, 0 for a violation ceiling -- and guessing the direction would fail healthy commands. That axis stays unmeasured and is recorded as such.
  • A CI gate authorized a dirty tree because git failed: the shared changed-file helper returned the same empty list for git-error, git-missing and git-timeout as for a clean tree. changed_files.get_changed_files returns list[str], a type with no channel for "I could not ask git", and all 19 caller modules read the empty list as the literal fact that nothing changed. The returncode != 0 branch did not even call log_swallowed -- that failure was discarded with no record anywhere. Measured in a repository with a genuinely modified tracked file and GIT_INDEX_FILE pointed at a garbage file, so git diff --name-only exited 128: roam adversarial --fail-on-critical printed "VERDICT: No changes detected" and exited 0, its --json envelope asserted changed_files: 0, partial_success: false, and roam pr-diff --fail-on-degradation printed "No changed files detected." and exited 0. Reproduced independently with git removed from PATH. The correct behaviour already existed in this repo on a PRIVATE helper -- cmd_delete_check._git_diff returns (diff_text, error_kind) and refuses under --ci -- and had simply never reached the shared one. A new get_changed_files_status returns (paths, error_kind) with git_not_available / git_timeout / git_error, the non-zero branch now logs, and the three callers that can authorize something read it: adversarial --fail-on-critical and pr-diff --fail-on-degradation publish summary.git_error with partial_success: true and exit 5, and reachability-triage refuses under --gate-on-new-reachable when the --range file scope could not be built, rather than filtering every flow away with an empty set. get_changed_files keeps its list signature so the 15 report-only callers are untouched. The narrowness is pinned by controls: a readable dirty tree and a readable clean tree both still exit 0. This graduates five strict-xfail pins the repo had already written against this exact defect, on their own stated exit conditions. What this does not close: pr-analyze --gate, cmd_diff, cmd_attest, cmd_test_gaps, cmd_affected_tests and cmd_affected still call the bare helper and their W805 pins remain xfailed -- a report-only command publishing an ambiguous empty change set is a disclosure defect rather than a false authorization, and pr-analyze needs a state-vocabulary change rather than an exit-code one; and pr-diff still emits no state field, so two of its sibling pins stay open.
  • The MCP server told agents to call a tool that cannot do what the instruction said. Its own instructions string opened with "TIP: call roam_expand_toolset first to scope tools to your task". roam_expand_toolset cannot scope anything from inside a session: _should_register_tool is consulted exactly once, at registration, so the tool surface is fixed when the server starts, and the meta-tool returns a list of what other presets contain plus the environment variable to restart with -- an action only the human operator can take. An agent that believed the tip spent a turn discovering it had been sent somewhere it could not act. Notably the tool's OWN description was already accurate ("List available presets... Call to discover tools beyond the active preset"); the false claim lived only in the text pointing at it, which is the harder place to notice because nothing about the tool looks wrong when you read the tool. The instruction now states what is true -- the surface is fixed at start, the meta-tool lists what the other presets hold, and selecting one means restarting with ROAM_MCP_PRESET=<name> -- so the narrow default still does not read as a dead end. Pinned by a test that checks the instruction against the program rather than against itself: it asserts the active-tool filter still has exactly one call site, so if the surface ever does become changeable at runtime the pin fails and the wording can be revisited when it would be TRUE. What this does not close: the tool keeps a name that describes an action it does not perform, because renaming a published MCP tool immediately after 14.0.0 would break configured clients for a wording problem; and genuine in-session expansion remains unbuilt -- it would need dynamic re-registration plus a tools/list_changed notification, which is a feature rather than a correction.
  • A whole-repo roam verify --report could report on part of the repo and call the result PASS. Report mode takes its targets FROM the index, so a tracked file the index has never seen cannot become a target, is never handed to the refresh pass (which only diffs the targets it is given), and is scored as if it did not exist. Measured in one repository at one commit: with one file indexed and a second tracked file containing a genuine syntax error, roam verify --report returned verdict PASS, score 100, files_checked 1, verification_complete true and index_refresh.state "current" -- a false CLEAN carrying a false claim of currency, over a file that does not parse. Running roam index and repeating gave FAIL 40 over 2 files from the same tree, same commit, same worktree. The non-report path never had this hole: it derives targets from the diff and treats a missing index row as a changed file, so a newly added file is indexed there. The sibling case was already guarded -- _all_source_paths refuses to spend an UNREADABLE index as "repo has no source files" -- and this is the same reasoning one step further: a PARTIAL index was being spent as "repo has only these files". Report mode now closes the gap before resolving targets, indexing tracked code files the index does not contain, using the indexer's own discovery and language detection rather than a second opinion about what counts as source. Repairing beats describing here: refusing instead would have turned every stale-index run into a non-PASS, which is honest but makes the ordinary case a failure. The repair is best effort by construction -- if the coverage question cannot be answered it changes nothing and reports zero, so a repository it cannot enumerate behaves exactly as before -- and it is idempotent, with a covered repo producing an identical verdict on a second run. What this does not close: the repaired count is not surfaced, so index_refresh reports current with a zero refresh count rather than naming the files it just added; the freshness field is now true when it says current, but it still does not tell a reader that a repair happened. And this covers report mode only -- an explicit path list still verifies exactly what it was given.
  • roam verify called valid TypeScript a syntax error, because a grammar that cannot parse a construct is not the same as code that is broken. Field reports from a production TypeScript application showed roam verify --auto returning a hard FAIL on a tree that passed the TypeScript compiler, a production bundle, and ~5,900 unit tests, with the culprit finding pointing at an ordinary import('...').Type[] annotation. Reproduced on a twelve-line file: syntax scored 50, the aggregate verdict was FAIL 40, and the flagged line was valid. The cause is upstream and precisely bounded -- measured against the bundled tree-sitter TypeScript grammar, import('x').Y parses, and applying ANY postfix to it does not: import('x').Y[], import('x').Y<T>, import('x').N.Y[] and readonly import('x').Y[] all produce ERROR nodes, while typeof import('x'), Array<import('x').Y> and a plain N.Y[] are fine. import() types are the standard way to reference a type without a circular import, so this is common modern code, and syntax is the check a reader trusts most absolutely -- a false positive there tells someone their working program is broken. roam cannot fix another project's grammar, but it can stop asserting more than it measured. When the grammar reports an error, these calls are now masked and the file is parsed again; if the second parse is clean, the construct was the whole complaint and nothing is reported. The mask substitutes an identifier of IDENTICAL byte length, so a genuine error is still reported at its true line and column on the retry -- verified: a file containing both an import-type array and a real unclosed bracket still fails, at the correct line. Replacing a parenthesised call with an identifier is valid in both type and value position, so the retry can only ever remove this one false positive; a file with no such call is not masked at all and its original verdict stands untouched. What this does not close: it is a targeted accommodation for one measured grammar gap, not a general policy, so the next construct the grammar cannot parse will be reported as a syntax error the same way; and the same field reports raise separate issues -- advisory findings driving a hard aggregate FAIL, whole-dirty-envelope scoring, alias/extensionless import resolution, and cross-module handler names treated as duplicates -- none of which this touches.
  • A leak catalogue that did not run was reported as a clean secrets check — the disclosure written to prevent exactly that was discarded one layer below the line that wrote it. _check_secrets sets repo_patterns_error under a comment reading "the repo catalogue did NOT run; disclose, never silently pass as if it had". _category_summary copies a fixed allowlist into the envelope, that key was not on it, and nothing else in the program ever read it — the field was write-only in production. Measured on a repository whose .roam-leak-patterns.py cannot be used: roam --json verify --report returned exit 0, verdict PASS, score 100, verification_complete true, a secrets category carrying exactly score/violation_count/violations, and no mention of the failure anywhere in the JSON. Every test covering this asserted on the dict _check_secrets returns, which is ABOVE the drop, so they were green throughout. The disclosure now reaches the envelope, and the tests that pin it assert on _category_summary output rather than the producer's own return value. Fixing the silence exposed a second decision the code had never made: _load_repo_leak_patterns returned one undifferentiated error string for two events that are not the same. Declining to execute untrusted repo config is this tool working as designed and is the DEFAULT for every repository that ships a catalogue without exporting ROAM_ALLOW_REPO_LEAK_PATTERNS=1; a catalogue the operator explicitly opted into and which then failed to load is a check that did not run. It now returns which one, and only the genuine failure sets execution_state, routing through the existing verification-gap path to a hard-blocking FAIL. Treating them alike in the other direction was measured, not imagined: marking the policy case incomplete made a repository that merely CONTAINS a catalogue verify FAIL — the same false verdict as the silence, pointed the other way. Four arms, all executed: opted-in and broken FAILs and names the exception; present-but-not-trusted PASSes and is disclosed; opted-in and working is clean and silent; no catalogue at all is untouched. What this does not close: the allowlist is still a hand-maintained list, so the next check that invents a disclosure key will be dropped the same way unless it is added here; and the sibling suffixed disclosures roam can emit (git_failed, index_refresh_failed, report_scope_discovery_failed, similarity_pass_skipped) were not audited for the same fate.
  • A gate that printed "nothing is proven clean" and then exited 0 — because the exit code was decided once per OUTPUT CHANNEL. roam ignore-drift --fail-on-found wrote its gate twice. The --json copy read "any violation OR an incomplete scan"; the text copy read "any violation", and sat below an early return that the UNANALYZABLE verdict never got past. On a machine where git could not answer — cwd not a worktree, git absent from PATH, a corrupt index file, a wedged git — the text channel printed the UNANALYZABLE verdict, printed that nothing had been measured, and authorized the push. Measured on one directory: text exited 0 while --json exited 5. Both of this repo's wired callers read the TEXT channel, and both restate the contract the text path broke in a comment directly above the invocation; the flag's own --help promises to exit 5 on UNANALYZABLE. Nothing but copy-paste discipline held the invariant — roam secrets is the proof in the other direction, writing the same expression three times, once per channel, all three correct. The fix is a single decision site rather than two agreeing ones: roam.exit_codes.gate_should_fail computes one boolean before the first channel branch and every channel reads it. CLEAN and VIOLATION are unchanged in both channels; only the unmeasured verdict moves, and it moves toward refusing.
  • Three CI gates named what they could not analyse and then passed it — in BOTH channels, which is why no parity check could see it. roam boundary --ci printed "no imports to analyze (corpus has 0 import edges)", roam taint --ci printed "22 rules loaded but not run" against an empty corpus, and roam test-hermeticity --ci printed "no Python test files indexed" — each exiting 0. A wrong-direction import cannot be counted in a corpus with no imports; zero findings from rules that never ran is not a security result; zero non-hermetic tests among zero tests is not hermeticity. Each now publishes scan_incomplete: true on that branch and refuses. That key is deliberately distinct from the partial_success these commands already emit, which is overloaded: boundary sets it for a clean run legitimately scoped to a changed range and taint sets it on a fully populated corpus with hundreds of findings, so gating on it would refuse every scoped run. Two of the three carried the same latent shape as the seed — a text tail whose early return skipped its own gate, and an empty-corpus branch that returned from both channels without consulting the flag at all.
  • The exit-code catalogue roam ships for CI scripts and agents described two codes no command returns. roam exit-codes self-describes as a table to branch on and is exposed as an MCP tool. Measured against the program: exit 3 is returned by nothing, because the only helper that raises it is called by no command and roam auto-indexes instead of refusing; exit 4 is never returned with its documented meaning, while the guard family really does return 4 for needs_review. So the code that never arrives carried index advice, and the code that does arrive got the index advice it must never get — the MCP layer reported a human-judgment gate to agents as a stale index, severity warning, and RETRYABLE, and a retry re-derives the same verdict. Exit 130 (Ctrl-C) was absent from the catalogue entirely, so a caller branching over the documented range falls through every arm when a user interrupts. All three are now described as they behave; no constant was renamed and no check was deleted to make a sentence true. The test that should have caught the misreport asserted the constant's NAME rather than what a caller receives, and was green.
  • roam doctor --help and roam guard-doctor each advertised an exit code no input can produce. doctor's help promised exit 1 for advisory-only failures; doctor has exactly two exit sites and both are exit 2, and advisory-only failures deliberately exit 0 so a fresh install does not read as broken — the code was right and the sentence was stale, in two separate docstrings plus one option help. guard-doctor promised exit 1 for an advisory failure; that rung is structurally unreachable because every failing check in the module is constructed as blocking, and non-blocking problems are emitted as warnings the exit decision does not read. A pipeline written as "if 1 warn, elif 2 fail" collapsed every advisory degradation into the success branch. The same blindness made the summary line contradict its own table — VERDICT: healthy printed directly above a warning row — and that is fixed; the verdict now reads warnings.
  • roam guard-pr --ci — the merge gate — printed a green verdict over a repository it could not open, and a caller could not tell that run from a healthy one. The change set is enumerated from git; the fallback returned an empty list both when git said "nothing changed" and when git refused to speak, and every layer downstream read the empty list as the former. The verification contract is derived from the change set, so an empty contract makes "all required passed" vacuously true. Measured in a worktree with a real uncommitted edit on disk and a corrupt .git: roam ignore-drift --fail-on-found exited 5 and roam secrets --fail-on-found exited 5, while roam guard-pr --ci — with --strict active, since --ci implies it — printed a pass verdict, "0 of 0 required checks ran", and exited 0 in all four channels. A HEALTHY copy of the same fixture produced the identical verdict line and the identical exit code; the only textual difference was the head sha in the provenance footer. The empty change set is now distinguished from an unreadable one at the point of measurement, and the unreadable case is a hard-gate verdict reason with the envelope publishing the same claim the exit code makes. The narrowness is deliberate and is pinned by a control test: "nothing was required of this change" remains an answer and still exits 0, exactly as pr-analyze --gate reporting no diff does.
  • roam rules-validate --strict advertised an exit code it could never return, and the command's two gate flags gave opposite answers about the same unmeasurable state. The help promised "exit 5 on any warning"; the flag computed a fail term that only if gate and fail ever read, so --strict alone could not change the answer of any run. With no rules file on disk, --gate exited 5 and --strict exited 0 while both printed VERDICT: load failed: file not found. This is the same class as the doctor/guard-doctor help-text defect fixed earlier in this section, live one command over. --strict is now a gate in its own right, the unreadable-file branch publishes scan_incomplete and refuses through the same single decision site, and reporting mode without either flag still exits 0.
  • roam taint --ci exited 0 when a rule filter matched no rules — a one-character typo turned the security gate into a no-op that reported success. --rules-pack is validated by click; --rule is a free substring filter and is not. --rule python-sqli found a finding and exited 5; --rule python-sqlii printed "No rules in ..." and exited 0. Zero findings out of zero rules is not evidence of zero taint. The empty-corpus branch of this same command was closed above; the zero-rules branch returns before ever reaching it, and was invisible to both new structural guards by construction — symmetric across channels, and publishing no completeness signal for the second law to read.

Added

  • Two structural guards for the class above, both demonstrated red against the broken tree rather than asserted. A registry-driven differential sweep runs every gate-flagged command in text, --json and --sarif across three environment classes — measurable-and-clean, measurable-with-a-real-finding, and unmeasurable-because-git-cannot-answer — and requires the same exit code from every channel, plus a refusal wherever the command's own envelope reports an incomplete scan. It enumerates from the command registry at collection time, so a newly added gate is covered without editing it, and it carries meta-guards so a discovery regex that stops matching fails loudly instead of passing vacuously. Alongside it, a static scan of every registered command module rejects the shape the seed shipped: a degradation name in the guard of a gate exit in one output-mode region while the sibling regions' gate exits ignore it. Measured at zero findings across the whole surface, so it ships with no allowlist — a future violation cannot be absorbed into an exemption nobody re-reads. The obvious stricter rule, "every channel's gate guard must be textually identical", was prototyped and rejected on measurement: it flags roughly eight commands of which seven are equivalent under normalisation.
  • The differential sweep above was itself attacked, and three of its own reports of coverage were not measurements. (a) Three of its 42 command/flag pairs died in argv parsing before the gate ran — a missing positional, a missing required option — so every channel exited 2, parity held because every channel was equally unmeasured, and the file reported green with no marker of any kind. A third law now asserts that a probed pair actually reaches its gate, and the pairs that cannot are pinned with their reason so the set fails when it grows. (b) The second law selected the envelope by POSITION, taking the last single-line JSON object on stdout; a command publishing an incomplete-scan claim in a pretty envelope and then one trailing hint line had the assertion read the hint, find nothing, and PASS — a silent authorization, not a skip. It now reads every summary the command published and holds it to any of them. (c) Its docstring claimed a newly added gate command is covered without editing the file. It is not: discovery is a heuristic over a flag-name vocabulary OR help text that documents an exit code, and a synthetic flag avoiding both, carrying the seed defect verbatim, was collected zero times. The claim is withdrawn and replaced with the measured arm split, and the vacuous-collapse floor is raised from a round number to the measured high-water mark, which previously tolerated a silent 17% loss of coverage.

[14.0.0] — 2026-08-07

> Install pins in this repository follow the PUBLISHED wheel, not the tag. Every install instruction here — 46 of them, enforced by scripts/sync_surface_counts.py and scripts/check_install_targets.py — named 13.10.0 when this section was tagged, because a pin may never name a version that cannot be fetched. They move to 14.0.0 via python scripts/sync_surface_counts.py --write after the 14.0.0 wheel is live on PyPI, not at tag time: _published_version() reads the LOCAL tag list, so running it at tag time would put 46 pins on main that 404 at the consumer — verbatim the defect check_install_targets.py was added in this release to prevent. Verify the move with python scripts/check_install_targets.py --network, which is the only form that asks PyPI; the offline default is satisfied by a local tag alone. > > Two consequences of that ordering are permanent in the v14.0.0 artifacts, and are stated here rather than left to be discovered. (1) The composite action as it exists at the v14.0.0 tag declares 13.10.0 as the default of its version input, because the pin bump lands on main after the tag and can never reach a tag that already exists. Referencing the action at that tag without setting version: therefore installs 13.10.0, not this release; set that input explicitly if you need 14.0.0 from that ref. (2) roam ci-setup run from the 14.0.0 wheel emits pipelines whose install line names 13.10.0, for the same reason and with the same remedy — edit the emitted pin, or re-run ci-setup from a later release. The wheel is built once from the tagged commit, so no post-tag repository edit can change what it emits. > > Neither sentence above may be written using a literal pin form: scripts/sync_surface_counts.py scans this file, and a pin-shaped literal here is rewritten by the very sweep this note describes. That is why this paragraph names versions in prose only.

Added

  • roam ignore-drift — the standard audit for tracked-but-ignored files reports clean, always, and this is the form that does not. Every repo that ever added a .gitignore rule retroactively holds files git still tracks under a rule that claims to exclude them; gitignore governs what git picks up, never what it already holds. The natural audit — git ls-files | xargs git check-ignore — returns zero hits in every repository, because git check-ignore silently skips paths that are in the index unless --no-index is passed. It reports CLEAN on exactly the defect it is hunting. Measured across three repositories on 2026-08-05: the naive form found 0 in every one; the --no-index form found 43 tracked-but-ignored files in one (42 of them under a single directory, including a 2.6 MB corpus) and 27 in another (including a credentials file tracked since 2025-09-17 under a rule naming it). Both had been "audited clean" before. The command ships with --fail-on-found, and it does not ship alone: it runs in scripts/prepush_check.py beside the two sibling leak gates and in the CI secret-scan workflow, so a --no-verify bypass or a push from a clone without hooks still hits it. A detector nothing invokes is a script someone has to remember to run, which is the same posture as not having it.
  • scripts/check_install_targets.py — a gate that fails when a documented install target does not EXIST, and refuses rather than passing when it cannot tell. Its sibling sync_surface_counts.py proves every install pin names the same version; nothing proved that version could be fetched. Three outcomes, not two: exit 0 OK, exit 1 FAIL, exit 2 UNKNOWN. Every way of not knowing returns 2 — git unusable; an EMPTY tag list (a shallow clone has none, and "no tags" is not "no releases"); a tracked file that would not open; a scanner that matched nothing; a shipped CI template carrying an UNPINNED install, whose target is whatever is latest at run time and so cannot be checked at all; a registry that did not answer; and a registry answer that is not the registry's own JSON for the version asked about. Only a clean 404 counts as evidence of absence. It is offline by default and sub-second, so it runs on the push path and in CI rather than at publish time, where a truth check cannot prevent the lie it detects.

Three of those refusals exist because the first version of this gate reproduced, in its own code, the defect class it was written to prevent — and each was found by attacking it rather than by running it. (a) The empty tag list was documented as UNKNOWN in three places and implemented as FAIL: the empty set flowed into the membership test, every pin came back missing, and a plain git clone --depth 1 was told that 13.10.0 — which demonstrably exists — "does not exist". A false assertion of ABSENCE built from missing data is the same defect as a false assertion of presence with the sign flipped. Its test asserted != OK where every sibling asserted == UNKNOWN, and FAIL satisfies != OK, so twelve green tests coexisted with a contract the code never honoured. (b) --pypi decided existence on 200 <= status < 300 and never read the body. An intercepting proxy answers 200, and urllib's default opener honours https_proxy from the environment — so an empty body, a captive-portal page, malformed JSON, a redirect to another host, a 204, and a payload describing a different version all certified that an unpublished version existed. Measured against a local server, all six returned exit 0 before and exit 2 after, with a valid-JSON control still returning 0. The status is now required to be exactly 200, the final URL to still be the host asked, the content type to be JSON, the body to parse, and info.version to equal the version asked about. (c) A shipped template with no pin at all is invisible to a pin scanner — nothing to rewrite, nothing to check, nothing in the count — so the gate reported OK about a file it never evaluated. templates/examples/roam-guard-pr.jenkinsfile was exactly that: pip install --quiet roam-code, unpinned, the only member of a five-template family without a pin, while its README described all five as equivalent drop-ins. It is now pinned wheel-only with a post-install version assertion, and the gate refuses on any shipped template that loses its pin.

Two further reaches were added rather than assumed. The offline check reads the LOCAL tag list, which a tag created and not yet pushed satisfies while every consumer's action ref still resolves to nothing — precisely the state the release path passes through — so --remote asks GitHub for the ref and --network runs both halves. And the report now carries its denominator: scanned N of M tracked files with each skip class counted, because "46 pins are fine" says nothing about the 2,709 files the sweep declined to read. A tracked file that will not open is now UNKNOWN rather than zero pins, and a file whose bytes are not valid UTF-8 is decoded with replacement instead of skipped, so an ASCII pin inside it is still seen.

  • roam review-request / roam review-accept / roam review-verify — a cross-family review verdict becomes a verified artifact a runner outside the agent can hold, instead of a claim the agent makes about itself. review-request emits the brief to hand a different-family reviewer; it carries the criteria and the artifact and deliberately NOT the author's rationale, because a reviewer given the defence tends to grade the defence. review-accept records the outcome as a receipt bound to the artifact's RAW bytes — raw, because the normalisation an earlier version applied first was non-injective, and two different artifacts that normalise alike could share a receipt. review-verify re-derives the verdict from the artifact's CURRENT bytes, so a receipt stops applying the moment the plan or the diff it reviewed changes underneath it. roam.review_receipt.verify_receipt is the only producer of a review result the verdict gate will read; there is no path that accepts an asserted status. New modules: src/roam/commands/cmd_review.py and src/roam/review_receipt.py.
  • roam verdict gained a SECOND blocking axis — and it stays off for every bundle that predates it. Until now a verdict blocked on evidence: a required check that did not run, or one that ran without being recorded as passing. It now also blocks on an unfulfilled cross-family REVIEW obligation, through _collect_review_obligation_blockers in src/roam/verdict.py, emitting plan_critique_not_run, done_verdict_not_run or review_receipt_missing. The legacy-safety property is structural rather than a flag, which is the part worth checking before you upgrade: the gate is ACTIVE only when the work itself declared obligations — the envelope's own orchestration_contract, which the caller cannot waive by passing nothing — or when the caller opted in explicitly by passing review evidence. Work that declares no obligations and whose caller passes nothing keeps its legacy verdict, and that is every proof-bundle path that shipped before this gate existed; in practice the axis activates for bundles produced by the new roam compile and for nothing else. The remedy is the three commands above, in order: roam review-request, then roam review-accept, then roam review-verify. The gate's own docstring records the limit it does not close — the contract reaches it through the same bundle the agent authors, so an agent that strips the contract from its own bundle escapes it. That is the general shape of self-reported evidence and is not closable inside a local library; it needs a component outside the agent's write authority, such as CI recomputing the contract from the envelope. Naming it in the docstring keeps the gate from reading as stronger than it is.
  • roam compile edit-context envelopes carry a phased execution contract, and the envelope now declares the version its shape actually has. execution_contract_for attaches the five-line phased tuple only when the envelope precedes an EDIT, judged by the compiler's own _is_edit_context signal — the same one that gates edit-probe injection — so query and read-only envelopes are not made to mandate phased edits. The 1b/4b review obligations ride an additive orchestration_contract block rather than arriving as sixth and seventh contract lines, for two reasons: the five-line tuple is pinned by drift guards asserting its exact length and wording, and these obligations carry policy plus criteria-template ids that a contract line cannot express, because each names a REVIEWER rather than a step. Both fields are additive and ABSENT — never empty — when not carried, so schema_version moves 1.1.0 -> 1.2.0 to describe what roam actually emits while leaving 1.1.0 consumers unaffected, which is why it is a minor rather than a break. Compile-time envelopes deliberately carry no artifact hashes: the agent plan and the diff do not exist yet, and a placeholder there is precisely what a later claim could pass off as a frozen value.
  • roam compatibility gained --require-coverage and --accept-removals, and now runs as a blocking CI job rather than a thing someone remembers to run. A surface the baseline does not record cannot be reported as removed later, so a gap in the baseline's reach is a hole in the gate itself; --require-coverage exits 5 (EXIT_GATE_FAILURE) when the baseline does not record the whole current surface, which forces a surface change and its baseline refresh to land together instead of drifting apart. In the same spirit --write-baseline now refuses with exit 5 when the snapshot it is about to write would drop entries the existing baseline records, and names --accept-removals as the way to say so deliberately — regenerating a baseline until the diff goes away is the failure mode that flag exists to make visible. Two steps in .github/workflows/roam-ci.yml run it against dev/compatibility-baseline.json: one fails on a removed command, flag, envelope field or MCP tool, the other fails when the baseline no longer records the whole shipped surface.
  • roam guard-pr discloses whether its gate was actually enforced. exit_code alone is 0 in two very different situations — the verdict was fine, and the verdict was blocking but this run was not gating — so the JSON envelope's summary now carries gate_enforced, gate_suppressed and verdict_exit_code. A blocking verdict that ran unenforced also writes a stderr banner naming the exact flag that suppressed it, so the human reading the terminal and the machine reading the envelope learn the same fact.
  • canonical_procedures() in src/roam/plan/compiler.py — the canonical procedure set is published as a frozenset[str] instead of being inferred by consumers from whatever surface they could reach, which made the count a thing each consumer rediscovered and could get wrong independently.

Breaking — read before upgrading

Three CLI flags are REMOVED, and the rest of this release is behavioural. An earlier draft of this section said there were zero surface removals; that was written before the removal landed and is corrected here rather than left to be discovered on upgrade. roam api-changes --changed, roam budget --staged and roam compile --model-tier no longer exist. A caller who passes one now gets a click UsageError and exit 2 — Error: No such option: --changed, Error: No such option: --staged Did you mean --range?, Error: No such option: --model-tier — on a command line that worked before. Nothing was renamed, no MCP tool disappeared, and no MCP preset narrowed. Against the PRE-REFRESH baseline roam compatibility --json reported removed=3 and exit 5; dev/compatibility-baseline.json was refreshed as part of this release (see below), so the same command run on this tree now reports removed=0 and verdict: no regressions. Do not read that zero as "nothing was removed" — read it as "the baseline has caught up". Their MCP mirrors went with them (roam_budget_check(staged), roam_compile(model_tier)), which is recorded under Fixed below because the gate could not see that half at all.

An earlier draft of this paragraph added "and three is the whole of it", citing that same removed=3. That sentence is WITHDRAWN, and the reason is worth more than the sentence was. roam compatibility detects a closed enum — removed/renamed/added commands, removed/added per-command flags, MCP tools/params/presets — and names what it does not evaluate on every run: cli_categories, cli_command_implementation_targets, cli_flag_types_and_defaults, mcp_tool_parameter_types_and_defaults, mcp_tool_descriptions, runtime_behavior. A flag COMBINATION that is newly rejected removes no flag, so it is invisible to a flag-removal diff by construction; that removed=3 was true and proved nothing about completeness. Citing a gate's silence as evidence of absence is this release's own headline defect, and it had been reproduced inside the notes describing it. Treat every enumeration in this section as a lower bound established by targeted measurement, not as a closed set. Two entries below were found only after that correction, by diffing command behaviour rather than command surface.

Two invocations that exited 0 at 13.10.0 now exit 2, and neither removes a flag. Both flags still exist, so the surface gate cannot see either.

  • roam verify --changed FILE... is now rejected. --changed scopes verify to the git diff; passing explicit FILES as well was accepted and one of the two scopes silently won. It now raises INVALID_OPTIONS: --changed scopes verify to the git diff, but explicit FILES were also given and exits 2. Remedy: split it — roam verify --changed for the diff, or roam verify FILE... for those paths. A script that passed both was getting one of them and not being told which.
  • roam mutate move|rename --apply --dry-run is now rejected (--apply and --dry-run are mutually exclusive, exit 2) where it previously exited 0 and rewrote your source files — the defect recorded under Fixed below. The Fixed entry states what it used to do wrongly; this one states what it does now, because a caller whose script passes both flags needs the second fact and not the first. Remedy: drop --apply to preview, drop --dry-run to write.

One text-mode output contract moved, on a command that shipped in 13.10.0. roam compile "<task shorter than the classifier's floor>" used to print VERDICT: task_too_short on stderr; it now prints a full VERDICT: facts_envelope for freeform_explore envelope on stdout, carrying injection_advice: skip_task_too_short where the old verdict string was. Exit code is 0 in both. JSON mode is unchanged — --json still emits summary.verdict == "task_too_short" under schema roam-compile-error-v1 — so only consumers that grep the human text are affected. Remedy: read injection_advice, or use --json, which was always the stable surface.

Additive envelope keys — and nothing removed. Truncated envelopes now carry summary.emitted_counts ({collection: count}), so a consumer can tell how much of each collection survived the budget rather than inferring it from length. That is the one worth planning against, and it is not the only one: a sweep of every command that takes no required argument (210 of them) run under --json at 13.10.0 and again here found 33 further additive summary keys and 10 additive top-level keys — among them secrets' fail-closed disclosure counters, compatibility's covered/uncovered dimension blocks, health's god_component_thresholds, init/index's corpus and state, taint's evidence_mix, and budget's metrics_version. The same sweep found zero envelope keys removed at any level — no summary key, no top-level key, no agent_contract key — and no schema string changed except roam schema's own payload version (1.1.0 -> 1.2.0). Additive, so nothing breaks; recorded because an agent-facing schema addition that appears in no changelog is a surface nobody can plan against.

Each of the three was a no-op, which is why removal beats repair — measured, not asserted, because the measurement is the entire basis for not reverting. Against the pre-removal source bytes taken straight from git (git show 2a95e2a0:<path>, compiled rather than imported, so an editable install cannot shadow the result), each parameter is present in co_varnames and is the argval of zero load instructions in the command's own code object or in any nested one: budget/staged LOADs=[], api_changes_cmd/changed_only LOADs=[], compile_/model_tier LOADs=[]. The probe carries a positive control, without which a clean result would prove only that the probe is blind — budget/explain, api_changes_cmd/base and compile_/artifact are parameters that are read, and all three show LOAD_FAST. The remaining back-doors are closed by construction rather than by inspection: none of the three signatures has **kwargs or *args (co_flags VARKEYWORDS and VARARGS both false), none of the three parameters is a cell variable, so no nested function can capture it (co_cellvars=() on all three), and git grep -n "ctx.params\|locals()" 2a95e2a0 -- src exits 1 with zero matches, so there is no generic parameter back-door anywhere in the tree. A parameter that is never loaded cannot reach behaviour. The user-visible consequence is exactly the error, never a different result.

Remedies, one line each. api-changes has no wider or narrower mode to select: its only file source is git diff --name-only <base>, so the narrowing --changed advertised was already unconditional and dropping the flag changes nothing but the error — delete it from your command line. budget compares two whole-tree metric snapshots and there is no staged-scoped metric to collect, so --staged scored the entire working tree while claiming to be scoped — delete it; the result you were getting is the result you keep. compile selects an artifact on procedure and classifier confidence only, with no model-tier concept anywhere in the plan layer; pass --artifact to choose an envelope shape explicitly.

dev/compatibility-baseline.json was refreshed for these three entries and for nothing else, deliberately rather than silently. The refresh went through the tool's own --accept-removals override, which exists precisely because regenerating a baseline until the diff disappears is the failure it is meant to make visible. The gate was exit 5 before — VERDICT: breaking changes (removed=3 renamed=0 added=0 breaking=3 coverage_gap=0) — and the file diff is five lines: three flag entries deleted, plus one reflowed line where "--range" lost a trailing comma. Nothing else was added, nothing else was dropped, and --require-coverage still exits 0, so the baseline's reach was not reduced to make the count go down.

The other half of the major is BEHAVIOURAL, and it is one mechanism repeated across the fixes below: a check that could not run used to report that it had run and found nothing. An absent measurement resolved to a benign value instead of to unknown — (), [], count=0, severity="ok", score=100, VERDICT: ... clean — so a gate that never executed came back green. Six of the fixes share a sharper variant worth stating on its own: a value crossed a boundary without the identity of the producer that made it, and the receiver's default for "producer identity ABSENT" was "producer identity MATCHES" rather than "unknown". Every fix converts an implicit equality, or an implicit pass, into an explicit UNKNOWN that fails closed. The consequence for you is that runs which exited 0 can now exit non-zero on the same inputs, on the same command line, with no flag changed.

Commands whose exit code can newly be non-zero where it was 0 along this axis — the two rejected flag combinations above are a different axis and are not repeated here, and this list is what targeted measurement found rather than a closed set: roam verdict (a required check with no recorded PASSING status no longer satisfies the requirement), roam fitness (a rule whose type no checker handles is a failure, not a silently disabled rule), roam preflight (a checker that raised is not a rule that passed), roam laws check --strict, roam secrets --fail-on-found, roam py-types --ci, roam cga verify (an unrunnable dirty-tree probe is UNKNOWN, and is no longer rendered as either a clean tree or as tampering), roam guard-pr, and roam pr-analyze --gate --cache. A wider set keeps its exit code but stops printing a clean verdict over a scan that did not complete — roam adversarial, roam doctor, roam health, roam sbom and roam vuln-reach among them; the non-degraded stdout path is byte-identical, and the disclosure goes to stderr and INTO the SARIF document rather than beside it, because a warning printed next to a SARIF file is not in the file the gate ingests. roam cga emit does not gain a failing exit, but it now signs a third value for the dirty-tree probe instead of None, so predicates emitted on a box without git are no longer indistinguishable from predicates emitted over a clean tree.

Three of these carry a real upgrade hazard, and each has a short remedy.

1. roam secrets --fail-on-found now fails closed on FOUR conditions rather than one, and the one most likely to bite you is a stale index. It still blocks on a finding. It additionally blocks on a --severity floor set above the highest severity the pattern table can emit — a filter under which no finding could have matched regardless of what is in the code, previously reported as "No secrets found"; on zero files having actually been read; and on any file present on disk but absent from the index. That last one is the hazard, because ensure_index() builds the index only when the database is ABSENT, or was left incomplete by an interrupted build, and never refreshes a stale one. One non-ignored file added since your last roam index therefore turns a previously green gate into exit 5, with NOT PROVEN CLEAN: N indexed files scanned, but M file(s) present on disk are not in the index and were NOT scanned. The remedy is one line: run roam index before the gate. The new behaviour is the correct one — the old green result was a clean bill of health covering files nothing ever opened — but it is a workflow change riding along with a bug fix, not just a bug fix.
