CI checkouts that build the index in-process on every run are unaffected, because there is no stale index there to be stale. 2. roam laws check --strict now decodes UTF-16, so a --diff-file that previously scored "0 violations" may newly report REAL violations on an unchanged command line. PowerShell 5.1 writes UTF-16LE by default, so git diff > x.patch on Windows produced a file that the previous read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace") turned into a BOM replacement character followed by the real text interleaved with NULs. Measured on the pre-fix code, same diff, both encodings: UTF-8 gave 1 file parsed and 6 added lines; UTF-16 gave 0 files parsed and 0 added lines — with error=None in both cases. Every line of the mangled text classified as other, so no file was ever opened and no law saw a single added symbol, and the run ended VERDICT: 0 violations and exit 0 from a strict gate over a diff it never read. The existing fail-closed guard did not catch it because it keys on not diff_text.strip(), and text full of U+FFFD and NULs is not whitespace. The reading is now the repo's hardened decode_views set (BOM dispatch, NUL-stripped, byte-transparent), so a genuine UTF-16 diff is evaluated correctly rather than refused — which is the better outcome and also means violations that were always present in your diff can surface for the first time on an upgrade. Bytes that yield no diff structure under any reading are returned as an ERROR into the existing "DIFF UNAVAILABLE — no laws were evaluated" path, which sets partial_success and exits EXIT_GATE_FAILURE under --strict; that also covers a wrong file passed to --diff-file, a truncated download, and a context-format diff the parser does not speak. An empty or whitespace-only file is still NOT an error, because an empty diff is a real, well-formed answer meaning "no changes". 3. roam pr-analyze --gate --cache will recompute verdicts it would previously have served from cache, and your first run after upgrading is a cold cache by construction. The cache key hashed diff text, the rules file, the block threshold, the language override and a CACHE_VERSION whose own comment scopes it to "bump when the envelope shape changes" — so every term was an input or a serialization tag, and nothing named the producer. The cached value is summary.verdict, which _serve_from_cache turns into sys.exit(EXIT_GATE_BLOCK). Measured with one set of inputs and a fresh process either side of a change to the module that derives the verdict, the key was byte-identical before and after, and a bundle written by the old logic was served under the new logic's key as {'cache_hit': True, 'summary': {'verdict': 'SAFE'}} — so the gate could pass or fail a PR on a verdict the running code never computed. The key now carries an analyzer fingerprint: mtimes of every module in roam.commands.pr_analyze and cmd_pr_analyze, discovered via pkgutil so a module added later needs no maintainer discipline, plus the installed-version stamp. Neither term alone is sufficient. The practical effect is that a PR passing on a cached SAFE may block the first time the current code actually evaluates it.

Fixed

  • roam doctor measured that a file existed and published the cause "a git process was killed mid-write". git repo health reported .git/index.lock as stale on presence alone. git holds that lock for the duration of every normal index write, so a lock created moments ago is a LIVE writer — the one state the message rules out. Presence was measured; death was inferred. The check's own comment said it: "the lock's presence is the finding; its age is only flavour." Age is not flavour — it is the entire difference between a writer and a corpse. Because the check is BLOCKING, the inference had teeth: under pytest-xdist roam doctor exited 2 on a healthy repository, taking one CI lane red at a commit the other three passed, twice in one day, and a false positive about a healthy repo blocked this release. Now three-way, and only the middle case changed: younger than the threshold is a live writer and is not reported; older is stale and reports exactly as before; an age that cannot be read still reports, because a failed stat cannot prove the lock is live. The threshold is generous on purpose — an abandoned lock is permanent, so a late report costs nothing, while a live lock called stale costs a failed run every time any tooling touches git in parallel. The cheaper fix was rejected: widening the test's accepted exit codes would have hidden this from CI while leaving it live for every user, and blinded the same assertion to a real blocking failure later. The test file's own docstring already said "every positive case has a matching 'must not fire' pair" — this check was the one shipped without its pair, which is why it shipped wrong. It has one now. Not closed: the unreadable-age branch has no test; driving it needs Path.stat to fail for one path, but Path.exists() is implemented via stat, so any patch reaching the branch defeats the guard before it.
  • Two CVEs landed against a pinned CI tool between one push and the next. pypdf 6.14.2 acquired CVE-2026-71852 and CVE-2026-71870 on 2026-08-07, both fixed in 6.15.0. Nothing here changed to cause it — one commit passed the dependency-audit lane and the next failed it with only changelog files in between; the advisories were published in the gap. The gate behaved correctly and is not the defect: pip-audit --strict fails on ANY known vulnerability in the locked graph, which is the point of auditing a locked graph rather than trusting it. All four Python lanes failed identically, which is how this was told apart from the single-lane index.lock race above. pypdf is CI-only, so no shipped artifact carried the vulnerable version. It is bumped rather than waived, for the reason the pillow pin already records: dev-only code is still installed in CI and must audit clean. The ci-group drift guard then caught its own group changing — it pins the exact literal in two places so a version cannot move in pyproject.toml alone, and it refused a change that touched one file and not the other.
  • The Jenkins example told readers to commit the secret that authorises their builds. templates/examples/roam-guard-pr.jenkinsfile set the Generic Webhook Trigger's token as a literal inside its GenericTrigger block. In that plugin the token is not an identifier — it is the shared secret in the invocation URL (/generic-webhook-trigger/invoke?token=…), so anyone able to read the file could fire builds on any Jenkins that used the template as written, and being used as written is what a template is for. It now reads tokenCredentialId: 'roam-guard-webhook-token', the plugin's own indirection, with the credential stated as a requirement in the file header. Deleting the setting was not an option and the comment at the call site says so: a GenericTrigger carrying neither token nor tokenCredentialId accepts UNAUTHENTICATED invocations, which is worse than a published one. This repository's own pre-push secret scan is what caught it — it had been in the file since it was written, and surfaced only when an unrelated commit rewrote the file and made the blob new in a push range. It was not suppressed with the scanner's # secretsallow marker: the finding was true, and silencing a true positive to make a push succeed is the failure these gates exist to prevent. Fixing it at the tip was also not enough — the scan reads pushed HISTORY, so the literal had to leave every commit in the range, which is why the unpushed commits were rebased. No wheel-shipped template was affected: src/roam/templates/ci/Jenkinsfile has no triggers block, measured rather than assumed. What this does not close: no test asserts the absence of inline trigger tokens across the example family, so a future template can reintroduce one and only the secret scan will object, and only once that blob changes.
  • The version pins on public main told every reader and every machine to install a release that did not exist, and the gate that runs on every push is what wrote them. scripts/sync_surface_counts.py held one belief about version literals: that each must equal pyproject.toml -> version. That is true of literals that DESCRIBE this artifact and false of literals that INSTRUCT a fetch, and the two were one class. So the moment 14.0.0 was declared, the sweep rewrote ~50 install instructions to name it and reported "All release-version pins match pyproject 14.0.0" — while the pip pin returned HTTP 404 from PyPI and the action ref resolved to no ref at all. The worst instances shipped INTO A USER'S REPOSITORY: roam ci-setup --write and roam init --with-ci=github emit files the user commits, and those files carried a pip pin and an action ref that both fail at the user's CI runtime. Reproduced end to end before and after in a scratch repository. The class is now split — identity literals (CITATION.cff, codemeta.json, the plugin manifest, server.json's own version, generated doc headers) still track pyproject; install literals (the pip pins, the action refs, the composite action's version input and default, server.json's packages[].version, the roam-guard post-install equality assertion) track the last PUBLISHED release, i.e. the highest v* tag. _published_version() refuses when the tag list is empty or unreachable rather than falling back to the declared version, because that fallback is the defect. .github/workflows/roam.yml loses its exemption: it was the one file that got this right, and it is now correct by construction rather than by exception.
  • A light reindex left every edited symbol invisible to lexical search — 11.4% of this corpus, with no error, no warning and no degraded-mode disclosure. Indexer.run(light=True), the path roam verify takes after every edit, skipped phase 7 entirely. But phase 1 CASCADE-deletes an edited file's symbols and re-inserts them under fresh AUTOINCREMENT ids, so skipping the phase left the new ids with no symbol_fts row while the old rowids lingered as orphans holding pre-edit text. _FTS5_SEARCH_SQL inner-joins symbols ON sf.rowid = s.id, so an orphan row is dropped and a symbol without a row can never be returned. Measured on the roam-code index: 5,174 symbols missing from FTS and 4,012 orphan rows, worth roughly 13 points of recall@20. Row COUNTS cannot detect this — an in-place edit keeps the count identical — which is why the check is on the id sets rather than on the totals.
  • roam init printed "Roam is ready: N files, 0 symbols, 0 edges" and exited 0 for six structurally different situations, four of them broken. An absent measurement rendered as a definite success value, in the first command a new user runs. It had already produced one wrong conclusion in this estate: a measurement run against a venv that had indexed 0 rows got green results from every indexing-dependent assertion. Init now distinguishes the legitimate empty cases (empty repo, docs-only repo, everything excluded by .roamignore or .gitignore — each now NAMED) from the broken ones. The refinement matters as much as the refusal: "files in a supported language and no symbols" is also true of an empty __init__.py beside an import-only module, which parses perfectly and declares nothing, so the refusal keys on a corpus that understood nothing rather than on a corpus that found nothing.
  • A per-process parse-error counter made one bad file refuse every later index in the same process. parse_errors was module state nothing ever reset, harmless while it only fed a log line — until the corpus verdict started reading it to decide an exit code. Index a file with a syntax error and every subsequent index in that process inherited the count and was refused as a broken corpus. A one-shot CLI never sees it; in-process callers do, and it cost 358 errors plus 32 failures across the empty-corpus suites, all as setup failures. The guard around tree.root_node.has_error for older tree-sitter bindings was fixed in the same area for the same reason: swallowing that AttributeError made every file look clean and downgraded a refusal into a false success, on the counter that decides whether a zero-symbol index is an empty tree or a broken one.
  • An extraction changed which count gates the vector rebuild. Pulling the rowid diff out of build_fts_index into _sync_fts_rowids returned rows-INSERTED and branched the TF-IDF/ONNX rebuild on that; the original branched on the FRESH ID SET. The two differ whenever a symbol lacks a surviving files row, and the branches pass different labels and different exc_types to _build_vector_signals — so the divergence silently changed which ONNX exceptions get logged rather than propagated. The sync now returns (deleted, fresh_count, inserted) and gates on fresh_count, restoring the pre-refactor branch exactly while callers reporting work done still get the truthful inserted count.
  • --budget 0 promised unlimited in three help strings and was the value that capped. click default=0 plus _apply_envelope_budget honouring only budget > 0 meant an explicitly typed 0 fell through to the default cap. Measured: roam --budget 0 taint --json returned truncated: true, budget_tokens: 20000, summary.findings: 894 and ten findings in the payload.
  • roam mutate move / roam mutate rename rewrote source files under --apply --dry-run. Both declared --dry-run, bound it into the signature, and never read it; the write decision was recomputed from --apply alone. With no flags the default is already a preview, so nothing ever looked wrong — which is why it survived. An explicit preview that writes is the one direction of this defect that costs the user their working tree.
  • Six more flags were accepted from the user and then silently discarded, found by scripts/audit_dead_cli_flags.py and each hand-checked against **kwargs forwarding, ctx.params, locals() and nested-closure rebinds before being touched, because the auditor is an AST name-usage heuristic and says so. The dispositions were not two but four, and an earlier draft of this line named only two — which concealed the one that can break a caller's script. One was WIRED (roam file --full); three named nothing the command could do and were REMOVED (the entries under Breaking above); one, roam init --yes, is KEPT as a documented no-op; and one, roam verify --changed combined with explicit FILES, became a REJECTION of a previously-accepted invocation and is recorded under Breaking above with its remedy. A flag that is neither wired nor removed is the disposition a "wired or removed" sentence cannot express, so it silently fell out of the account.
  • roam taint published intra-function co-occurrence as proven source-to-sink dataflow, at confidence: high, risk_score: 100, and a fabricated three-hop path — 891 of 894 findings on this repo carried path_length: 3 for a path nobody walked. The JSON envelope was made honest first; the SARIF projection of the same finding is corrected under its own entry below, because SARIF is the surface a Code Scanning gate actually ingests.
  • The RELEASE-tier linkcheck gate could not fail. scripts/linkcheck.py gates its exit code on --strict; without it the script prints every dead link and anchor it found and still exits 0. The tier registered it flagless and GateRunner._run records PASS on returncode 0, so the gate reported green on a broken landing page — while CI ran the --strict form. A tier that advertises itself as "what CI verifies" and runs a weaker form of the same command is worse than one that does not run it at all.
  • The pre-push hook ran whatever python PATH resolved to, not the project's interpreter. Measured on a dev box: PATH-python was a global 3.14 and the gate failed a correct push over 7 test errors in dependencies that do not exist under the project's 3.12 venv. A gate that blocks on an environment nothing ships teaches people to reach for --no-verify, which is the one habit the hook exists to make unnecessary.
  • roam verify on a clean tree printed VERDICT: PASS (score 100/100) and OK — all checks passed having run zero checks. checks_run was [] and files_checked was 0 on that branch. The human-facing lines are corrected here; the agent-facing agent_contract block — the one the MCP tool returns verbatim — is corrected under its own entry below, because fixing the text and leaving the contract would have repaired the surface nobody's automation reads.
  • is_test_file matched its test-directory list with a bare substring, and the anchored replacement was wrong in BOTH directions. The first fix replaced an unanchored in over the whole lowercased path with an exact / delimiter / camelCase component match; two independent adversarial reviews then refuted it on measured real files. Scored against a 20-row refutation corpus: legacy substring 13/20, the anchored replacement 0/20 — worse than what it replaced — and the shipped form 18/20, with the two remaining misses named in the source rather than left implied. Recorded as a pair because the intermediate state is the lesson: an anchoring that is obviously more correct than a substring can still be strictly worse than it, and only a refutation corpus says which.
  • Three distribution manifests were read by three different publication channels and swept for drift by none of them. .claude-plugin/plugin.json sat four releases behind on a field the plugin host treats as the UPDATE TRIGGER, so every installed copy was frozen on an old manifest, mcpServers block included. It was not forgotten once, it was unreachable: the value carries no pin shape, so the shape-anchored sweep could not see it, and it was in no count registry either. It and the two citation manifests are now covered structurally. Separately, a release bumped the machine-read version fields and left five human-readable prose captions quoting the prior release — two of which are consumed by downstream tooling rather than only read by humans.
  • A published benchmark number that no reproduction confirms is not a result. bench/retrieve/SUBMISSION.md is public, opens with "Quick reproduce", and told the reader to run a command; three different recall sets existed in the repo and nothing re-derived any of them. All of it was re-measured on a named commit with a fresh full index and the numbers replaced with what that run produced.
  • The surface-compatibility gate counted MCP presets and never read their MEMBERSHIP. _COVERED_DIMENSIONS listed mcp_preset_counts and _UNCOVERED_DIMENSIONS did not list membership, so membership sat in neither — the harder shape to notice, because a number WAS recorded and diffed and the claim over "presets" read as complete. A count is a lossy projection of a set. Reproduced pre-fix by swapping one real member of the core preset for another real tool at an unchanged count of 17: the snapshots were byte-identical.
  • The guard on the pre-push RELEASE note could not see a gate whose result decides control flow. _unconditional_gate_labels filtered candidate statements by KIND — only ast.Expr — so a runner.<gate>(...) call in value position was never a candidate, which is house style in that very file. Widened to read the value position too. The residual reach of that extractor is now stated where it is claimed rather than implied; see the entry below.
  • Two release guards asserted a frozen version literal and so failed a correct release for no defect. A hardcoded number in a pin guard cannot distinguish the release it guards from the bug it catches: it agrees with a template that never got bumped (shipping the previous wheel to every consumer, green) and disagrees with one that was bumped correctly (red, no defect). The direction of the signal is inverted precisely when it matters. Both now derive their expectation — and, since the pin class split above, they derive it from the LAST PUBLISHED release rather than from the declared one, which is a different number for the whole bump-to-release window.
  • The surface-compatibility gate printed surface_coverage: "complete" and 0 entries outside baseline coverage over a dimension it could not read at all, and the commit directly above this one in the changelog is the proof. dev/compatibility-baseline.json recorded mcp_tools as a flat list of 244 names with no parameters, so a removed MCP tool parameter was outside the gate's reach by construction. The three-flag removal recorded above also removed the two MCP wrapper mirrors of those flags — staged from roam_budget_check, model_tier from roam_compile — in the same commit. The CLI half went exit 5 and forced a deliberate roll-forward; the MCP half passed the same gate in the same run. Snapshots built from the two revisions were byte-identical at 5,833 bytes, and running the shipped gate across that pair with --ci --require-coverage gave VERDICT: no regressions (removed=0 renamed=0 added=0 breaking=0 coverage_gap=0), exit 0. Two parameters vanished and the artifact could not tell the two builds apart. That is not an unmeasured claim, it is an unfalsifiable one, which is why the fix had to be two-sided. coverage_gap sums additions across the dimensions the snapshot collects, so a dimension the snapshot never collects contributes zero no matter what happened to it — the completeness assertion could not have gone red. So the measurement was widened: the snapshot is now schema 1.1.0 and records mcp_tools as {tool: [parameter, ...]} (244 tools, 936 parameters, +17,591 bytes on a 69,235-byte artifact, +25.4%), removed_mcp_tool_params is the sixth term of the breaking tally, and the same real pair now reports VERDICT: breaking changes (removed=2 ... breaking=2) naming roam_budget_check(staged) and roam_compile(model_tier), exit 5. The parameter diff lives inside _diff rather than in a wrapper, so --write-baseline's ratchet inherits parameter-erasure refusal exactly the way it inherits graceful-rename handling. And the claim that remained was narrowed to what it measures. Even with parameters recorded, complete is a statement about recorded dimensions, so the envelope now publishes covered_dimensions (6) and uncovered_dimensions (5) beside it, surface_coverage_scope: "covered_dimensions", and both lists in agent_contract.facts — and the text output prints them on every run including a clean one, because a clean run is exactly when "no regressions" gets read as "nothing regressed". Each covered dimension is asserted to move the verdict when perturbed and cli_categories is asserted not to, so neither list is prose. A pre-1.1.0 baseline is treated as unrecorded rather than as "no parameters": it counts 244 into coverage_gap, flips surface_coverage to partial, and fails --require-coverage with exit 5. Reading the absent key as an empty one would have reproduced this defect one schema version later.
  • roam --json verify --changed on a clean tree told an agent PASS, score 100 — having run zero checks — in the one block the MCP tool returns verbatim. The human-facing lines were made honest earlier; the agent-facing agent_contract was not, and it is the block that actually reaches the primary consumer, because the MCP tool roam_verify shells this exact command and returns the envelope with no post-processing of agent_contract. Measured on a clean tree before the fix: facts was ["PASS", "score 100", "70 threshold findings", "0 files checked", "violation count 0"] and risks was [], beside summary.checks_run == [], summary.files_checked == 0 and summary.state == "no_changes". An agent that reads the bounded contract block — which is what the block exists for, and what a context-tight agent is told to read instead of the full payload — came away with a verdict and a quality score for work nobody did, and an empty risk list that reads as "no concerns". It now reads NOT VERIFIED: 0 of 35 checks ran / 0 files checked / state no_changes: no file was read and no check ran / threshold 70 was never applied to any file / score 100 is the not-run default, not a measured result, with two risks naming the same thing. The check count is derived from _ALL_CHECKS rather than written down, so registering a check cannot turn the fact into a false count. The wire numbers deliberately did not move, and summary gained nothing. compile verify shells this command and validates the result against a pinned no-changes contract that requires summary.score == 100 and categories[*].score == 100; separately, its _require_known_shape(summary, allowed=_VERIFY_SUMMARY_KEYS) is a CLOSED key set, so an added summary key would raise summary_schema and exit EXIT_TOOLCHAIN on every clean tree. The disclosure therefore lands in agent_contract, which that boundary only requires to be a dict. The nine-key summary set is now pinned by a test, so a later "let's just add a field" cannot break the boundary quietly, and the four machine-readable not-run discriminators (state, files_checked, checks_run, violation_count) are unchanged.
  • {"threshold": N} rendered as "N threshold findings" in every agent-facing fact that carried it — a gate setting read as a count of findings. The fact humaniser classifies a summary key as either a measurement name ("health score 75") or a count noun ("5 critical findings"); threshold fell through to the count-noun rule, so roam verify's threshold: 70 became the fact 70 threshold findings, which states that seventy things were found. Measured blast radius: 40 "threshold": summary entries across 14 command modules (cmd_check_rules, cmd_compiler_health, cmd_complexity, cmd_context, cmd_diff, cmd_docs_coverage, cmd_drift, cmd_envelope_diff, cmd_fitness, cmd_health, cmd_over_fetch, cmd_smells, cmd_verify, cmd_watch), all emitting the same garble. threshold is now a measurement-naming suffix and the fact reads threshold 70. That list had three copies and a guard covering only two of them. The humaniser's measurement_suffixes, agent_opt._MEASUREMENT_SUFFIXES (the runtime weak-fact detector) and the CI lint's hand-maintained mirror must agree, or the lint rejects the string the humaniser just produced. Parity between the latter two was already pinned; the copy that decides how a fact is actually rendered was not covered by anything, which is how a suffix added to two of three would have gone unnoticed. A new test AST-reads the humaniser's list out of the source — deliberately not importing it, since it is a function local and since two names for one object is not a parity check — and asserts set equality with the lint's, naming which side each drifted entry is on.
  • roam taint --sarif published the claim roam taint --json disclaims, on the same index and the same finding. The JSON envelope is honest about what the analyser did: all 637 findings on this repo carry confidence: low, reason: "source and sink co-occur in the same enclosing function; no dataflow path was computed", evidence: "co_occurrence", path_length: null, and a risk_score of 0 that excludes every one of them. The SARIF projection of that same finding came out as level: "error", message Tainted flow: environ → run, and a three-step codeFlows threadFlow — and a codeFlow is the assertion that those hops were walked. They were not: cmd_taint builds path from f.path_symbols for every finding, so a co-occurrence entry carries a synthesised source/enclosing-symbol/sink triple, and that triple is what became the threadFlow. SARIF is the machine-read surface a Code Scanning gate consumes, so it is where a fabricated flow does the most damage — 637 co-occurrence hits presented as 637 proved injections, at the one severity that fails a build. A finding whose evidence is present and not dataflow is now published without a codeFlows entry, never at level: "error", with a message that names the basis (Possible tainted flow (co-occurrence only; no dataflow path was computed): environ → run), and with properties.evidence / evidence_detail / path_length so a triage user can see what it rests on. Measured before and after on the same index: level counts went from 637 error to 633 warning + 4 note, codeFlows present went 637 → 0, result count unchanged at 637, document still parses and still reports version 2.1.0. The downgrade is conditional, and the condition is evidence — not confidence. confidence and reason are attached downstream by wrap_findings and are absent from the findings_dump dicts the emitter receives, so keying off them would have been a no-op. A genuine evidence: dataflow finding keeps its level, its Tainted flow: message and its codeFlow byte-for-byte; this repo produces zero dataflow findings today, so that regression would have been invisible without the synthetic case now pinned in tests/test_sarif_flag.py. An absent evidence key is treated as unknown and changes nothing — cmd_taint stamps the field on every entry it builds, so every finding roam actually emits takes an informed branch, and manufacturing a disclaimer out of a missing field would be the same fabrication pointed the other way. That choice is pinned by its own test rather than left to inference.
  • The co-occurrence disclosure was deleted by the warning that came after it. cmd_taint appends "N of M finding(s) rest on co-occurrence only …" to summary.warnings_out, then the qualified_only rules-lint branch assigned the same key with a bare = instead of appending — so any run producing both signals shipped the lint warning and silently dropped the sentence that qualifies every finding in the envelope. Every neighbouring branch in that block (zero-anchor rules, W607-AY/CJ substrate markers) already reads-then-appends, which is what makes this an omission rather than a convention. On this repo rules_lint.qualified_only_violations is 0, so the branch never fired and the live disclosure survived; the defect is reachability, and tests/test_r3_taint_cooccurrence_disclosure.py forces both signals into one run to hold it. A second test pins the substrate markers in their terminal position so the change cannot reorder them.
  • The pre-push gate disclaimed a gate it had just run. On success the RELEASE tier of scripts/prepush_check.py prints a list of CI lanes that "are NOT run by any tier and stay unproven here", so an operator does not read local green as "CI will be green". One entry in that list was false: it named roam ignore-drift --fail-on-found, which _run_leak_gate registers and which main() invokes unconditionally before any tier branching — so it runs in FAST, FULL and RELEASE alike. Measured on a live FAST run: [prepush] roam ignore-drift --fail-on-found: PASS (0.4s). A note that disclaims proven work is worse than no note, because the reader's only correct response to "unproven" is to spend a CI round proving it. The bullet is narrowed to roam secrets --fail-on-found, which is the only one of secret-scan.yml's three steps genuinely absent from the push path — the other two, the repo leak-catalogue scan and this tracked-but-ignored gate, both run in every tier. The gate itself is untouched; making the sentence true by deleting the check would have been the same defect pointed the other way. A regression test pins THIS instance, and the class it did not close is closed by the entry directly below. AGENTS.md carried the same claim and is corrected to match. Its release-discipline section listed secret-scan among the lanes the release tier leaves uncovered; it now names the single step that is uncovered and says the other two run in every tier. The guard that was built to prove that note honest could read 7 of the 8 gates a live run records, and the note is now DERIVED rather than guarded. The first version AST-walked main() for runner.<gate>() calls, collected the labels those methods pass to self._run(...), and asserted no label appeared in a bullet. It was widened twice and it was still bounded by syntax: a keyword-argument call, an aliased receiver, a starred argv, a non-literal label, a module-level helper and an inline results.append(...) all evaded it, six shapes found in one probing session with no terminating condition on the search. Two of those shapes were LIVE in the tree — run_pytest_bundle builds its label with an f-string, which is why 8 gates ran and 7 could be named, and run_release_temp_capacity_gate appends its result inline. The shape that settles it is not a syntax at all: a correctly-written positional literal placed under if release: is skipped as "not unconditional" and passes, while the note it certifies is printed ONLY in the RELEASE tier. No widening of a reader reaches that, because the defect is in the predicate rather than in the parsing. So the disclaimed-lane list became data (_RELEASE_UNPROVEN_LANES) and _print_summary filters it against runner.results — the list it already receives as its first parameter — printing (no longer unproven: … — ran as …) rather than silently shortening itself, because a suppression with no stated cause reads as an edit rather than a measurement. That makes the class impossible by construction instead of detected after the fact. All eight shapes above, including the tier-placement one, were confirmed RED against the pre-derivation script and green after. What it does NOT close, stated because narrowing a claim twice is not a fix: a bullet is still related to a gate by SUBSTRING, one hand-maintained probe per bullet; it closes only the FALSE-disclaimer direction, so a CI lane added to .github/workflows and never disclaimed at all remains invisible to any runtime record and would need a different guard over workflow YAML; and a red gate truncates the record, which is correct for a note describing what THIS run proved but means the note must be computed in-process at print time. AGENTS.md held a fourth hand-maintained copy of the lane list and now points at the note instead of restating it.
  • The guard built to prove that note honest could not read the wiring shape main() already uses, so the note could have gone false again with the guard green. _unconditional_gate_labels learned a gate's label only by resolving runner.<method>() to a FunctionDef and walking THAT function for self._run("<label>", ...). A gate wired as runner._run("<label>", ...) directly in main() resolves method='_run', walks GateRunner._run, finds no nested self._run inside it, and contributes nothing. Measured on a copy of the script carrying one extra unconditional runner._run("roam compatibility --ci", ...) — a label the note's own bullet list already disclaims: the guard read the same 7 labels as the real tree and passed. The extractor now reads the direct form too, and on that same mutated tree reads 8 and fails with 'roam compatibility --ci' is registered by main() but disclaimed in the bullet 'roam compatibility --ci / --require-coverage'. On the real tree it reads the same 7 labels as before and stays green — a strict widening of the measurement, not a new finding. The evading shape is the next move the note itself anticipates, and the widening is bounded so it cannot over-fire. roam compatibility --ci / --require-coverage is a live bullet in that "NOT run by any tier" list, and wiring that lane into the push path is the obvious follow-up to the compatibility work above. A negative control pins the other direction: the identical runner._run(...) nested under if release: is not collected — 7 labels, green — because those lanes genuinely do not run in FAST and the note is right to disclaim them. All 5 runner._run(...) calls in main() today are inside if release: and 0 are direct children of its body, so the widening changes nothing about the current tree; it closes the shape before something occupies it. The extractor's own blindness tripwire did not fire on the shape that blinded it, so the tripwire moved to the output. assert unconditional_methods was written for "the AST shape this guard reads has changed and the guard is now blind" — but runner._run(...) IS a runner.<method>() call, so on a main() whose always-on gates are all direct-form the assertion sees ['_run'], passes, and the extractor still returns zero labels. The verdict is labels ∩ bullets == ∅, which is vacuously true on an empty set, so the guard then certifies the note with maximum confidence having read nothing at all. Measured on such a tree: zero labels, tripwire silent, verdict green. The assertion is now on the labels actually read, so an extractor that reads nothing fails loudly instead of certifying silence — including for a third wiring shape neither branch anticipates. Both properties are pinned by tests over a fixture carrying all three wirings (grouped, direct, tier-conditional), and both were confirmed RED against the pre-widening extractor and green after.
  • The guard on the pre-push script was not run by the pre-push script, while its own docstring said it was. tests/test_prepush_gate_wired.py opens with "This module pins the contract via pure AST inspection (no subprocess, no index build) so it runs in the FAST bundle itself". Measured: a --collect-only over FAST_PYTEST_GUARDS returned 0 node ids from that file, and it was absent from FULL_PYTEST_GUARDS too. So every contract it pins — the bundle membership list, the once-and-only-once whole-tree leak scan, and the RELEASE note not disclaiming a gate that runs in every tier — was enforced by CI after the push and by nothing before it, while the docstring read as local coverage. The widening directly above is worth nothing on the push path if the guard carrying it does not run there. The claim is made true rather than deleted, and the file now pins its own membership. test_prepush_gate_wired.py joins FAST_PYTEST_GUARDS, and it is added to this file's own _EXPECTED_FAST_GUARDS set, so dropping it out of the bundle fails the guard instead of quietly restoring the gap. The same --collect-only now returns 10 node ids. Measured cost, same box and same 4-worker pool: FAST pytest bundle 58.1s → 59.1s, whole FAST tier 94.1s → 94.6s — one second for the file it guards, which is exactly the file whose change should run it.
  • CONTRIBUTING.md documented a version-sync guarantee the repo did not provide, and the next release would have shipped an action that installs the previous release. The claim was that pyproject.toml is the single source of truth and "everything else syncs from it via scripts/sync_surface_counts.py". That script synchronises surface counts; it contained no version handling at all, so the version half of the sentence had never been true. The consequence is not cosmetic: action.yml's version input default and server.json's PyPI package pin are the fields that decide what a downstream consumer actually installs, so a release that bumped pyproject.toml alone would publish a composite action whose default installs the version before the one just released, and tell the MCP registry to fetch the same stale wheel. The stale claim survived for the same reason the underlying gap did — nothing ever failed on it. A survey of the tracked tree found 52 files carrying the release literal, not the 15 the section implied, including the entire shipped-CI-template family and four copy-paste guard examples. Crucially they are not one kind of thing, and a find-replace across them would have been a worse defect than the staleness: recorded benchmark measurements and a dated sample audit deliverable name the version they were produced by, so re-stamping them falsifies a result; the repo's own workflow pins its own published action and therefore cannot point at a tag that does not exist yet; and the compile-cache modules' version literals turned out to be narrative in comments (proven with the tokenizer, and now pinned as such) because the runtime stamp is read from the installed dist-info directory name — bumping a literal there would have been a cache-key behaviour change wearing a version sync's clothes. The fix extends the script CI already runs rather than adding a new one, so the documented sentence becomes true instead of being deleted. Pin detection is shape-anchored, not value-anchored — it matches the form of an install pin rather than the current literal — so a new surface is covered the day it lands rather than the day someone remembers to register it, and prose that merely names a past version is untouched by construction. Sites with no reusable shape (an action input default, a registry package pin, generated doc headers, landing-page version stamps that the existing landing-page sweep did not recognise) are anchored individually on surrounding structure so they cannot match anything else. Everything excluded is excluded by an explicit registry that must carry a reason, and a stale entry naming a file that no longer exists is itself a failure. Two assertions in the composite-action security suite that compared against a hardcoded literal now compare against pyproject.toml, turning them from restatements of the mistake into the invariant they were meant to express. Regression suite in tests/test_w1501_release_version_pins.py, built around controls in both directions: the negative control proves the gate reports each derived shape when it disagrees and that --write converges, and the false-positive controls — a CircleCI config schema version, a pinned third-party action version, changelog prose naming a shipped release, a recorded benchmark engine version, and a PEP 440 grammar example inside an error message — prove the sweep leaves non-pins alone, which is what makes it safe to run with --write during a release. Verified against a clean checkout rather than the working tree: the gate exits 0 on the true tree, exits 1 naming file and line when one derived occurrence is reverted, and exits 1 across every derived surface when the version is bumped with nothing else touched.
  • Six more places where a check that could not run reported that it had run and found nothing — found by a detector built from our own fixed defects rather than from intuition. verify-imports returned a zero-result SARIF document for a file it could not read, so a stale index turned every hidden unresolved import into a green gate on a scan that never happened; the projection gains an unverifiable-file rule (defaultLevel: warning) so the artifact a CI system ingests says the file was skipped rather than saying nothing. dead-public-surface treated an unreadable package manifest as "no public entry points", which is indistinguishable from a package that genuinely exports nothing — the difference between "this symbol is dead" and "I could not tell", published under the same word; unresolvable status now carries an unverifiable prefix that consumers must treat as UNKNOWN, never as proof of publicness and never as proof of deadness. test-hermeticity counted a file it failed to parse as examined, suppress treated an unreadable suppression store as an empty one (so a corrupt store silently disabled every suppression while reporting success), aibom published a symbol count of zero for an index it could not open, and article-12-check reported its high-risk scan complete over a truncated file set. Each is the same substitution the other fixes in this release share — an absent measurement resolved to a benign value instead of to unknown — and each now fails closed with the shortfall named in its own envelope. How they were found is the more interesting part, and it produced a result worth recording even though nothing shipped from it. Twenty-four defects of this class fixed in this release were mined out of git into a labelled corpus, each with its pre-fix code recovered by git show <commit>~1:<path>, so candidate detection rules could be scored on whether they actually catch defects known to have existed rather than on whether they sound plausible. The measurement produced a hard ceiling, stated before any rule ran: 8 of the 24 are closed to static analysis by construction, because the compare-side family is a MISSING TERM in a key or a comparison and absence has no syntax — sha256(label + "" + canon) is a well-formed expression, and what makes it a defect is a term that is not there, which cannot be pattern-matched without already knowing which terms belong, that being exactly the knowledge the defective code failed to write down. One instance is unreachable by any code analysis whatsoever, since the defect lives in a docstring's shell command interacting with redirect semantics and no line of Python is wrong. The realistic ceiling is 10-12 of 24 at usable precision, and any headline recall above ~67% on this corpus would mean the detector was matching something other than syntax. A cardinality trap was flagged in the same pass: one corpus row anchors on a single file but its commit fixed 59 modules of identical shape, so counting sites rather than commits would let that one row dominate every recall number.
  • roam budget would have exited 5 for every user on their first run after upgrading, on a tree where nothing had changed. Three unreleased fixes move numbers already written into .roam/index.db, and roam budget compares live metrics against the newest stored snapshots row. With shipped defaults its No new cycles: max_increase 0 rule sees the one-time step and fails the build. It is cycles, not health_score — cycles go UP while tangle_ratio goes DOWN, because the fabricated edges had fused unrelated code into a single ~1,500-symbol strongly-connected component; breaking it yields many small genuine cycles with far fewer symbols trapped in each. The gate is a metrics_version stamp on the snapshot row, and the granularity was chosen by measurement rather than by argument: an earlier proposal versioned the health SCORE, but collect_metrics produces a byte-identical dict under the pre- and post-unification code on the same database, so the score formula moved nothing while the graph moved everything. The movement is entirely index-time, zero read-time — a score-version stamp would have caught none of it. Rows written before the stamp read as version 1 and every consumer now refuses to compare across a mismatch rather than comparing anyway: budget skips every rule and exits 0 with the reason disclosed; health --baseline suppresses the WHOLE delta through the same branch as a missing baseline (partial suppression would leave cycles reading as a real regression alongside phantom improvements on the LIMIT-capped columns); fitness, alerts, forecast and bisect truncate at the boundary and say so, which matters most for bisect, where a drop in edge count is classified as degradation and the fix would otherwise rank as the top culprit commit in every user's history; and the workspace aggregator stops silently averaging two definitions of health across a partly-reindexed workspace. Two consequences were found only by building it. The snapshot writer's DELETE is now version-aware — a same-definition row is a genuine duplicate, but a different-definition row is the only surviving evidence of what that commit scored under the old measurement, and deleting it would destroy the very data point a user needs. That change is only safe alongside a second one: find_before_snapshot selected WHERE git_commit = ? LIMIT 1 with no ORDER BY, so once a commit can hold two rows it returned whichever SQLite reached first — rowid order, i.e. the oldest and stalest. And open_db(readonly=True) does not run ensure_schema, so the first post-upgrade run of every read-only consumer still sees the old table: naming the new column in SQL crashed fitness and forecast with no such column and silently dropped health scores in the aggregator, until a capability probe was added at the three sites that name it explicitly. The falsification pass caught its own headline test being vacuous — the seeded baseline passed against pre-fix code too — so both budget tests now share one regressing baseline and differ only in the version stamp; a temporary probe written without the new symbols then failed 10 of 10 against pre-fix code, reproducing the incident verbatim.
  • Six silent-degradation defects closed, and together they name a sharper mechanism than the one they were collected under. They were gathered as instances of "a signal that could not be computed, rendered as one that came back clean" — which turns out to describe only three of them. Nothing failed to compute in the envelope cache, the snapshot comparison, or the attestation verifier; all three computed correctly and compared the wrong things. The mechanism that covers all six is narrower and greppable: a value crosses a boundary without the identity of the producer that made it, and the receiver's default for "producer identity absent" is "producer identity MATCHES" rather than "unknown". Absent resolved to equal instead of to unknown, every time. The compile-envelope cache key omitted the tool version, so two versions hashed equal and a post-upgrade run could be served a pre-upgrade contract. A snapshots row with no metrics version compared as the same definition. The CGA predicate carried no graph-builder identity, so a verifier assumed the same builder — and "same builder" is precisely what licenses the wording "edges changed since signing", which reads to a user as tampering rather than as the tool upgrade it was; that one looks inverse (it over-claims rather than under-claims) but is the identical substitution. decode_text(errors="replace") had no channel to say the decoded text was not the bytes on disk. And the disclosure ratchet's high-water mark had exactly one carrier — the file the documented regeneration command truncates before reading, so --baseline > baseline.json made the shell destroy the mark, json.loads("") raise, and the ceiling silently reset with its rationale replaced by a placeholder: the documented remedy for silent degradation, silently degrading. --baseline now writes the file itself and the redirect is gone from the contract. The fixes share a shape too, which is the real confirmation: each converts an implicit equality into an explicit UNKNOWN that fails closed. Two of the six were held back from an earlier commit for being wrong rather than incomplete, and both are fixed here: cmd_migration_plan hoisted the declaration of its warnings list out of the JSON branch while leaving the sole producer inside it, so the text branch echoed a guaranteed-empty list — silencing the scanner while disclosing nothing, a false clean of the false-clean detector; and cmd_supply_chain passed disclosures into the SARIF projector and wrapped the result, landing every marker in toolExecutionNotifications twice. Which half to keep was settled by execution rather than taste: the kwarg-only form fails when the projector itself raises, because only the wrap can salvage a floored {} into a valid zero-result run. An adversarial pass then found a hole in the new guard — a degenerate fix that discards every finding the moment any boundary degrades passed all five assertions, because they counted notifications and never pinned that the results survived. One added assertion closes it, and the lesson generalises: disclosing a degradation is not a licence to empty the document. Guards in seven new test files, each confirmed failing against its pre-fix code and each carrying a negative control; the CGA guard's control is load-bearing in the security sense — same builder version with changed edges must still fail as tampering, so the new version field cannot become an escape hatch for a real mismatch.
  • The disclosure scanner still truncated its own analysis silently, in three places, after being rebuilt to fail closed. W1455 gave it three-valued per-file status, a published denominator, a positive control and a non-zero exit on unanalyzable — and left three UNCOUNTED caps inside the walk. A file whose analysis hit one was not examined; it was partially examined, and still resolved to CLEAN. The denominator counted FILES, not completeness. The fix came from enumerating every early exit and splitting them into two classes, which is the part worth keeping: truncation abandons an enumeration already in progress and must taint the verdict, while resolution imprecision models Python approximately and uniformly for every file — tainting on that would mark all 275 modules partial and destroy the signal. So the closure cap now records budget.hit(...) and yields PARTIAL; the _MAX_DEPTH = 12 recursion cap was deleted rather than raised, because visited already guaranteed both termination and completeness and the number was only guarding the Python stack; and a third cap nobody had noticed — for _ in range(3) in _carried_tokens — now runs to convergence under len(funcs) + 1, which is a proof (one chain-edge per round) rather than a larger guess. Measured at HEAD, none of the three was load-bearing: each fired zero times, peak closure was 293 names against a 4,000 limit, peak depth was 10 against 12, and the full scan ran 15.07s capped versus 14.73s fully uncapped — noise. Two levels of headroom is one helper-chain refactor away from silently truncating a shipped module, which is why the cap was removed rather than increased. Two planted corpora prove the caps were hiding real findings: a 20-helper chain and an 8-return chain through a shared bucket both came back CLEAN before and VIOLATION after. A fourth instance of the same shape was found in the same file: _carried_mark swallowed OSError/ValueError and returned the CURRENT count as the ratchet mark — an unreadable ratchet silently RAISED the ratchet, so a gate that lost its own history quietly got easier. Only FileNotFoundError is now a first generation; anything else refuses to emit. A coverage hole surfaced too: the one-level glob(".py") meant commands/pr_analyze/.py was in no bucket at all — not clean, not violating, not skipped, simply absent — now four SKIPPED records. In cmd_secrets.py the same audit moved files_scanned += 1 below the read it was counting (it had been incremented before a scan_file that can swallow an OSError and return [], inflating the denominator with files never opened), added a read_errors channel so [] stops being two-valued, and closed the partition with files_filtered / files_undiscoverable. Shadowed definitions — 28 across 11 of 275 modules — are published as imprecision.shadowed_definition rather than gated, and the one-module-deep closure limit is deliberately given NO key, because publishing an unmeasured limit as 0 is the same fabricated denominator in a different costume. Guards in tests/test_w1459_uncounted_analysis_caps.py: 14 of 15 fail against the pre-fix code, and the 15th exists to PASS — it runs the pre-fix scanner over both planted corpora and asserts they come back clean, which is what makes the other two behavioural rather than structural.
  • roam impact returned a byte-identical answer for unrelated symbols, because an unguarded case-insensitive fallback fabricated a quarter of the call graph. relations.py resolved a reference in three steps, and step 3 was a case-insensitive lookup whose own comment reads "VFP and other case-insensitive langs" — with nothing checking the source file's language. It ran for every reference in every file, and this repository contains no FoxPro at all. The failure is worse than mis-resolution: steps 1-2 fail for any name not defined in the repository — stdlib, third-party, builtins — and step 3 then bound it to whatever indexed symbol happened to match case-insensitively. Path from pathlib alone manufactured ~3,435 edges onto an unrelated PATH constant in a throwaway dev script; across all case-fold edges, 85% had a source identifier with no exact-case definition anywhere in the index. Ground truth by re-parsing every Python source and checking real imports: 25.1% of edges were provably fake, concentrated by kind at 86% of reference and 88% of type_ref. The user-visible consequence was measured before and after on freshly built indexes. Before: roam impact PATH, roam impact open_db and roam impact json_envelope all reported 18,331 symbols, 40.7%, risk high — identical to the digit for a dev-script constant and the database-connection factory. After: 3 symbols / low, 14,444 / 32.0%, and 14,245 / 31.6% respectively. roam deps on that dev script reported 972 importers where grep finds the filename nowhere; it now reports 11, the residual belonging to a separate simple-name matching path. Graph-wide, edges fell 6.45%, the largest strongly-connected component collapsed 1,484 → 123, and the share of symbols claiming more than 30% of the repository as their blast radius went 53.5% → 7.0%. That last number is why this mattered beyond a bad metric: roam pr-risk emits a risk factor at blast_pct >= 20, which essentially every symbol satisfied at a fabricated 40.7%, so a manufactured number was the named driver of the "critical" verdict a human reads before deciding whether a change is safe. The fix is one guard, chosen by ablation over the real graph rather than by argument: a competing candidate that dropped cross-file reference/type_ref edges removed 2.7x more edges and moved the pathology only 48% → 47%, while this one captures ~92% of it for 6.6% of the edges. It is expressed as a registry property — LanguageExtractor.case_insensitive_identifiers, declared True only by FoxPro — rather than a hardcoded extension check, so the next case-insensitive language never touches the resolver. One trap worth recording: the registry import must be function-local, because roam.languages.registry imports roam.index.parser, and importing anything under roam.index executes relations — a module-level import passed a smoke test and two full index builds before breaking collection for every test module that reaches roam.languages first; both import orders are now asserted. Guards in tests/test_w1456_casefold_fallback_language_guard.py (8 tests), and the negative control there is the interesting one: it cannot fail against the pre-fix code by construction, since the fallback existed then too, so its falsifier is deletion — stripping step 3 from the fixed code fails both FoxPro tests, which is the proof it is load-bearing. There was zero local FoxPro resolver coverage before this. Two findings beyond the fix: type_ref is the largest single loser at −67% of that edge kind, not reference as first assumed; and Apex and SQL are genuinely case-insensitive languages registered here that do not declare the flag, deliberately left unchanged so the behaviour stays inside the measured ablation, with a drift test that now fails the moment anyone adds one — making that a conscious decision rather than a side effect. Migration: on the next index, 5,557 of 44,948 graph_metrics rows (12.4%) change degree and every row changes pagerank, since it is normalised across the whole graph. Fitness baselines, health-score history and stored pr-risk/attest scores all shift. This is the third change today that moves stored metrics, after the health-score unification and betweenness seeding; they should be released together behind one baseline refresh.
  • The symbol-graph cache was keyed on id(conn) and had no invalidation at all, so a long-lived process served a stale graph after every reindex — measured at 100 out of 100 trials. CPython reuses object ids once an object is freed, so a closed connection's cached graph could be handed to a different connection allocated into the same address. Reproduced in a fresh process, without pytest or its conftest cache-clearing: a strict ABABAB alternation collapsed 40 requests onto 3 connection ids and still produced zero wrong answers, because regular alternation pins each project to its own stable address — which is precisely why this stayed invisible — while the realistic irregular shape (AAABBBAABBBBAAAB, a session that works in one repo then switches) produced 8 wrong answers in 16 requests, with two ids each shared by both projects and one project served the other's symbols. The severity as originally framed is REFUTED, and that matters more than the finding. Cross-project aliasing is not reachable through MCP as currently wired: _run_roam routes any root other than "." to a subprocess with a fresh empty cache, covering the 262 root-parameterised tools; the one in-process root-parameterised DB path (roam_oracle_batch) uses raw SQL and never builds a graph; and batch_search/batch_get are pinned to the server's cwd. An MCP server process is effectively pinned to one project, so "one project's structure answering another project's queries" does not happen there today. What IS live is broader in reach: there was no invalidation of any kind, so a server that caches a graph for its process lifetime keeps answering from it after an external roam reindex rewrites the database — 100/100 stale pre-fix, 0/100 after. indexer.py does call clear_graph_cache(), but only inside the indexing process, which is never the one serving. The key is now the resolved main-database path (via PRAGMA database_list, normcased) plus a change stamp, and the choice of stamp was itself corrected by measurement: an initial attempt used mtime and size, and its own invalidation test caught it — three successive commits left st_mtime_ns and st_size byte-identical while SQLite's header change counter moved 2 → 3 → 4, because Windows defers file-time updates. The stamp is now the header change counter plus size plus the -wal stat; PRAGMA data_version was rejected because it is explicitly not comparable across connections, and cross-connection lookup is the entire point. In-memory databases are never cached, since an empty path would make them all collide on one key. Cost is 89.6µs against a 460ms cold build over 44,688 nodes — 0.0195% — and the hit rate improves, because path-keying reuses the graph deterministically where id-keying only hit by address luck: on a repeated single-project sequence, builds drop from 4 to 1 and hit rate rises 60% → 90%. Guards in tests/test_graph_cache_project_identity.py, 2 of 3 failing pre-fix; the aliasing test asserts the cache is non-empty at the moment of aliasing (so conftest's clearing cannot mask it) and that at least one genuine id recycle occurred (so it cannot pass vacuously), and the third is a negative control asserting the same project twice returns the identical object, which blocks "disable the cache" as a fix. Three other id(...)-keyed caches were audited and are safe, one of them — _FILE_TEXT_CACHE, already path-keyed after a 2026-07 CI flake — carrying the "KEY DISCIPLINE" comment that is the direct precedent for this fix. This defect class has now bitten this repository three times: tests/test_w1451_health_score_single_source.py carries a hand-rolled _reset_graph_cache() whose docstring describes it exactly, and workspace/aggregator.py already loops raw connect/close over multiple repositories in one process, one import away from the same bug.
  • The scanner that enforces "a degraded signal must be visible" could not tell a clean file from one it failed to parse — and neither could the function whose job is proving coverage. scripts/scan_disclosure_asymmetry.py backs the W1331 ratchet; scan_file did except (OSError, SyntaxError): return [] and enumerate_command_sites did except (OSError, SyntaxError): continue. Reproduced by copying a command module, appending def broken(:, and scanning: violations: [] and enumerated sites: [] — byte-identical to a clean repository, with the zero-baseline test asserting violations == [] and passing. A syntax error anywhere under src/roam/commands/ silently removed that file from the gate AND from the coverage proof. scripts/scan_snake_case_violations.py carried the same except SyntaxError: return [], and its consuming test held a private second copy of the scanner with the identical handler — two independent places for one detector to stop detecting; the test now imports the script. Both are rebuilt to a three-valued contract: every file resolves to CLEAN | VIOLATION | UNANALYZABLE | SKIPPED with a reason, and no path returns an empty result for a file it could not read. The scan publishes its own denominator (files_parsed / files_unanalyzable / files_skipped), which the consuming test asserts separately from violations == 0, so a parse regression fails loudly rather than quietly. Exit codes distinguish the cases the old scanner collapsed: 0 clean, 1 violations, 2 unanalyzable, 3 scanner untrustworthy — the last covering both a broken self-check and zero files parsed, because zero coverage is not zero violations. Every exception in the walk, including a crash inside the analyzer, is caught per file and recorded rather than aborting or silently continuing. The piece that makes this durable is a positive control run on every invocation: a planted sentinel command whose disclosure asymmetry must be found, paired with a symmetric twin that must stay silent — so "always fire" fails the control exactly as "never fire" does. If the sentinel is not detected the run reports BROKEN and exits 3 even with zero violations. The reasoning behind it is the general lesson: without a positive control, "0 findings" and "the detector stopped working" are the same output, which is precisely the defect class the scanner exists to prevent. Zero matches is now reported as checked 275 files, 0 violations, 0 unanalyzable, positive control OK — the disclosure is the count, not the silence. Also fixed: a dead skip-list in the snake-case scanner that compared rel_parts[0] against directory names while always scanning under src/, so it had never skipped anything; the baseline regenerates byte-identical, confirming the rewrite is finding-neutral, and an old-loop-versus-new-report comparison over the real tree returned an identical violation set. Measured exposure: zero. 275 command modules parsed, 0 unanalyzable; 625 files for the snake scanner, 0 unanalyzable. The gate was not lying — it was incapable of telling you if it were. Guards in tests/test_w1455_scanner_fails_closed.py, 24 of 24 confirmed failing pre-fix, plus 14 pre-fix failures across the consuming tests. Finally, the repaired scanner immediately caught a real asymmetry in a command shipped earlier the same day: roam review-verify emitted partial_success to its JSON envelope and nothing to text, so a human or a log-scraping pipeline read a NON-passing verification exactly as it read a clean one. The first fix disclosed to text alone — and the scanner caught that inversion too, which is the point of checking both directions; the marker is now built once, above the branch, and carried by both.
  • roam diff --fitness reported [PASS] for rules it had never checked — including trend, a rule type the system fully supports — and roam attest baked those false passes into SIGNED evidence. cmd_diff._collect_fitness_violations dispatched with an if/elif chain over dependency/metric/naming only. Anything else fell through to violations = [] and was then recorded status: "PASS". Unlike the sibling defects fixed alongside it, this was not a silent drop: the envelope positively asserted the rule had been checked and had passed. Measured against one rule file where roam fitness reports dependency FAIL, naming PASS, trend FAIL and a typo'd type ERROR, roam diff --fitness printed 4 rules, 3 passed, 1 failed with health-must-not-regress [PASS] — a trend rule that had never once been enforced on this path — alongside typoed-rule [PASS], a type nothing can enforce. cmd_preflight held its own copy of the same hole (its exception path was closed separately; this is the unknown-type path), so a typo'd rule vanished from rules_checked entirely: the user wrote 2 rules, the envelope said rules_checked: 1, severity: OK, exit 0. The amplifier is the part that matters: cmd_attest._collect_fitness_evidence consumes _collect_fitness_violations, so every false PASS was being written into signed attestation evidence — a cryptographically vouched claim that a rule passed when it was never run. Fixed by the same change, and verified emitting honest rows. Both sites now disclose rather than fail closed, and that was decided rather than copied: roam diff --fitness already exits 0 on a genuinely FAILING rule (measured), because diff is an informational blast-radius report while fitness is the gate — so borrowing the gate's exit-1 would make a config typo exit non-zero while the architectural violation it was written to catch exits zero, which is strictly stranger than the bug. The decisive second reason is mechanical: _collect_fitness_violations is a library function called behind except Exception, and SystemExit derives from BaseException, so it would escape that guard and take roam attest down on a typo — pinned by a test asserting the collector never raises SystemExit, with the exit-0-on-real-FAIL premise pinned in both files so the decision is revisited if that ever changes. The if/elif is gone: _SCOPED_CHECKERS is now a narrowing table over _CHECKERS, membership goes through the shared _resolve_checker, and the fall-through is inverted — a registered type with no diff-scoped variant runs the global checker and carries scope: "repository" (a trend rule is inherently unnarrowable, since snapshot history has no per-file projection, and disclosing the scope stops a repo-wide FAIL reading as "this diff caused it"), while an unknown type produces the ERROR row with scope: "not_evaluated". cmd_preflight routes unknown types into the errored_rules bucket that already existed rather than opening a parallel channel. Both files carry AST shape guards forbidding literal type comparisons and local _CHECKERS.get lookups, plus add/delete drift tests proving that registering a checker teaches each consumer and deregistering one turns it ERROR — so a fourth elif cannot pass. Suites in tests/test_w1453_diff_fitness_dispatch.py (22) and tests/test_w1453_preflight_unknown_rule_type.py (18): 29 of 40 confirmed failing pre-fix; the 11 green in both states are exactly the negative controls, the exit-0 premises, the shared-registry invariant, and the vacuously-true half of a drift pair whose sister fails. One related drift corrected while looking: output/sarif.py's fitness_to_sarif docstring hand-listed three rule types and omitted trend — harmless at runtime, since rule_id derives from the value, but the same hand-maintained-list hazard one layer down.
  • roam health --baseline reported progress that never happened, because the score was implemented twice and the two copies disagreed. cmd_health computed one number and commands/metrics_history.collect_metrics computed another; the second is what gets STORED in snapshots, and --baseline compares today's first against yesterday's second. Measured on the same database at the same instant: score 71 vs 64, tangle_ratio 0.0 vs 3.6, and on this repository's real stored snapshot the command reported verdict OK, score +2, "38 cycles fixed" — on a repo that had actually regressed. Post-fix the same comparison reads BAD, −5, +1 new cycle. Not a crash: a confident false report, in the one feature whose entire purpose is detecting real change. The divergence was isolated to a single numerator. total_symbols and the graph's node count are the same population, so fingerprint's 0.0359 and collect_metrics' 3.6 were one measurement differing only by ×100 — but cmd_health filtered its cycle set to actionable SCCs, of which 0 of 39 qualify, yielding 0.0 while the same envelope simultaneously reported cycles_total: 39. Self-contradictory in one document. collect_metrics is the correct one, and not merely because it is the stored one: its numerator matches its own published definition ("symbols inside non-trivial SCCs", with no actionability qualifier) and matches roam fingerprint. Both units are retained deliberately, because each is load-bearing somewhere — percent for .roam-gates.yml's tangle_max, the sigmoid scale and the stored column; fraction for fingerprint --compare's max_range: 1.0 — with the definition now stating which is which and a test asserting health_pct == fingerprint_frac × 100. The fix is a new roam.quality.health_score module owning tangle ratio, signal derivation, factor composition and the geometric mean, called by both sites, plus a guard that fails if the two ever diverge again — which is the part that makes it permanent, since two copies of a metric will always drift and nothing was comparing them. Four more divergences in the same family were found while unifying: --baseline compared len(actionable_cycles) against the stored all-SCC cycles column; its dead_exports delta used a Python-only test_* check against a stored column computed with the canonical multi-language predicate, a standing false delta on every Go, Java and JS repo; collect_metrics omitted the 10% imported-coverage factor that cmd_health applies; and it wrote (avg or 10)/10.0, silently rewriting a measured file-health average of 0.0 into a perfect factor — the same absence-versus-zero conflation, one line further down. User-visible consequence, stated plainly: this repository's health score moves 71 → 64, and projects configuring health_min between 65 and 71, or any tangle_max, may newly fail their gate. The gate is now honest. Other snapshots readers are unaffected: collect_metrics output is byte-identical pre and post, so trends, forecast, alerts, bisect and the workspace aggregator keep reading a column whose value and meaning are unchanged, with no historical discontinuity — the sole exception being projects with imported coverage data, which see a one-time step. roam understand and roam dashboard read collect_metrics and therefore disagreed with roam health by 7 points; they now agree exactly, and test_understand_health_band_parity.py was strengthened from band-agreement to score-equality, closing a duplication its own comment had been tracking as an open follow-up. Regression suite in tests/test_w1451_health_score_single_source.py: 8 of 12 failing pre-fix, verified in a detached worktree rather than by stashing, since the tree is shared. The negative control requires a clean fixture to score 60-100 and requires that adding a cycle LOWERS the score by the SAME amount at both call sites — so "make both return 0" cannot pass.
  • The pre-commit hook was written in bash but declared #!/bin/sh, so on Linux it aborted before running a single check. Line 143 tested [ -n "${STAGED_PY// /}" ] — a bash pattern substitution. Under dash, which is /bin/sh on Debian, Ubuntu and every Linux CI runner and build lane this project uses, that is not a subtle difference in behaviour but a parse error: dash: 1: Bad substitution. Verified directly on a Debian host where /bin/sh -> dash. Because it aborts at parse time it took the WHOLE hook down, so the ruff gate, the surface-count check, the changelog-drift check and the internal-index check never ran on any Linux commit — and the failure was total rather than partial, which is why nobody saw a partial-gate symptom to investigate. It survived because of where it was written: on Windows, git-bash makes /bin/sh bash, so the construct works perfectly on the author's machine and nowhere else. Replaced with [ -n "$(echo $STAGED_PY)" ], which relies only on POSIX word-splitting and gives identical results on all four inputs that matter (empty, whitespace-only, one file, many) — confirmed under real dash, not by reasoning about it. The guard is a STATIC scan rather than a runtime one, in tests/test_w1454_githooks_posix.py, and that choice is the point: running sh -n on the Windows host where this was authored invokes bash, which parses the broken line happily. A portability bug cannot be caught by executing on the platform that lacks the problem, so the test scans every #!/bin/sh hook for thirteen constructs POSIX sh does not have (${var//}, ${var^^}, [[ ]], =~, <<<, mapfile, local -a, and the rest), skipping any hook that declares bash honestly. It ignores comments and single-quoted spans so a comment explaining a bash-ism cannot trip it. Two negative controls make the scanner falsifiable in both directions: one feeds it the exact line that shipped and requires a hit — without it, a scanner whose regexes matched nothing would report the codebase clean — and one feeds it the POSIX replacement and requires silence. Confirmed failing against the pre-fix hook. Found while building a lander that runs each repo's own pre-push gate on a Linux box, i.e. by finally executing our own tooling somewhere other than the machine that wrote it.
  • Betweenness centrality was sampled without a seed, so every roam index produced different numbers for unchanged code — and those numbers feed the feature whose whole job is detecting change. nx.betweenness_centrality(G, k=k, normalized=False) approximates over k randomly-chosen pivots; with no seed=, each run drew a fresh sample. Measured on a copy of this repository's index (44,688 nodes, k=1,056 pivots = 2.36% sampling), across three back-to-back runs on identical input: 3,904 of 44,688 nodes changed value, median relative change 7.5% on those that moved, the positive-betweenness population swung 3,446 → 3,566 (Jaccard 0.759, ~25% churn), and the p70/p90 severity bands moved +11.5% and +9.4%. Every one of those differences is a roam health --baseline delta that no code change caused. The honest nuance, because it makes this smaller than it first looks: the head is stable and the tail is not. Top-10 and top-15 were identical in membership and order across all three runs, and since _BOTTLENECK_LIST_LIMIT is 15 and all fifteen sit ~70x above p90, this repository's displayed bottleneck table was already effectively deterministic. What genuinely moved with no code change was the betweenness value printed on each row (−6% to +54% on individual top-20 symbols), the disclosed population in showing_top_15_of_N, the p70/p90 figures in the JSON report, and all 44,688 stored rows. On a flatter repository whose top-15 are not saturated above p90, severity classifications flip outright. Fixed with a module constant BETWEENNESS_SEED = 1 at both call sites — a fixed seed rather than a repo-derived one on purpose: a content-derived seed would redraw the pivot set on every code change and fold fresh sampling noise straight back into the baseline diff this is meant to protect, while also breaking comparability across clones. End-to-end on the real 44.7k graph, two seeded runs now differ on 0 of 44,688 nodes. A sibling was found and fixed in graph/simulate.py, and its shape is the more instructive one: its bottlenecks COUNT was perfectly invariant across eight unseeded runs (104 every time) while the MEMBERSHIP churned to a Jaccard of 0.29 — roughly 71% different symbols behind an unchanging number. A stable aggregate concealing near-total content churn is its own species of false clean, and a count alone would never have revealed it. Audited the rest: partition.py, cmd_cut.py, clusters.py, spectral.py, cmd_split.py and cmd_why.py already seed; cycles.py and the exact no-k paths are deterministic by construction; and the n <= 1000 branch passes k=n. An earlier draft of this entry claimed that made small graphs safe, on the strength of six unseeded runs coming back bit-identical locally. CI refuted it on the first run — 4 distinct results in 4 attempts. k == n means every node is sampled, not that sampling is skipped: random.sample still returns a different PERMUTATION each call, and floating-point addition is not associative, so the same contributions accumulated in a different order differ in the low bits. There is therefore no graph size at which an unseeded call is safe, which strengthens the fix rather than narrowing it — and the local six-run agreement was luck being mistaken for evidence.
